news.title: Ketanji Brown Jackson Breaks With SCOTUS Voting Order as Election Looms
news.text: Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the sole dissenter in a new Supreme Court order that green-lit New Hampshire to fully ban student IDs for voting during November's midterm elections. In the order, Brown concluded, "I respectfully dissent because—even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming—I would not disturb a clearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State’s electoral processes." New Hampshire passed a law earlier this year that said student IDs were not an acceptable form of identification to get a ballot, the Associated Press (AP) reports. What We Know The High Court's order ultimately blocks students from using their school IDs as a backup, the AP says. New Hampshire's Republican Secretary of State David Scanlan barred the IDs from being an acceptable backup after the state passed the law, the AP reports. A judge first left the law to stand as is but reversed course earlier this month, prompting the emergency appeal. The emergency appeal in Scanlan's case was ultimately granted by the High Court on Thursday. Legal Counsel for The Coalition For Open Democracy, the plaintiff in the case, called the court's order "wrong." "The Court’s decision grants a stay which both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied, blocking an injunction that has now been in place for almost three weeks, injecting confusion into the election—precisely what the Purcell principle is supposed to prevent—and authorizing an unconstitutional policy that will deprive young voters of their right to vote. "We applaud Justice Jackson for her dissent, in which she stands for the Constitution, the right to vote, and a rational application of Purcell. We will continue to vigorously litigate this case in the defense of the fundamental right to vote of young voters across New Hampshire," the statement read. The order mentions the Purcell principle, which is a legal concept in election law in the United States that advises courts against altering voting rules too close to an election. The election related ruling comes just 12 days before the midterms. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. President Donald Trump lost New Hampshire during the 2024 presidential election to then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The state's open Senate seat is rated as lean Democrat by the Cook Political Report and the governor's race is rated likely Republican by the forecaster. Read The Order in Full Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The order comes less than two weeks ahead of midterm elections.

news.title: Trump Aides LaCivita, Blair Donate Bosnian Fee to Library
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Chris LaCivita and James Blair, two of President Trump’s election advisers, have donated their six-figure consulting fees from a controversial political assignment in Bosnia and Herzegovina to Trump’s presidential library, The Post has learned.

Trump was “gloating” and “very braggadocious” in private conversations this week after learning about the donation, according to a source. The reaction suggests that his initial anger toward LaCivita and Blair over their work in Eastern Europe has subsided.

A second source also confirmed that Trump was pleased by the donation.

Four sources confirmed the transfer. Two of them said Trump learned of the decision indirectly rather than from LaCivita or Blair themselves.

LaCivita, who co-led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and Blair, who served as a White House deputy chief of staff until May, are still likely to owe income taxes on the earnings. Sources said each man received more than $100,000 from the consulting work.

Trump had lashed out earlier this month after The New York Times reported that the pair, who hold senior positions at the MAGA Inc. super PAC, had traveled to support a political party in the ethnically Serbian Republika Srpska. They advised the ruling party, led by Milorad Dodik, during the region’s election, which the party won.

SEE ALSO: Kamala Harris Met With Silence at Mississippi Rally After Quote Flub

Dodik has friendly relationships with both Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The outside assignment created the impression that LaCivita and Blair were using their ties to Trump for personal financial gain while diverting attention from struggling Republican congressional campaigns. Some colleagues, however, said the two men remained involved in the US election effort remotely.

“Chris LaCivita and James Blair are outside consultants. They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in his initial response on Oct. 7.

“They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C. I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

Blair, who spearheaded a Republican redistricting effort this year aimed at reshaping House districts to benefit the GOP, joined Trump at a campaign rally in South Carolina on Wednesday. His appearance pointed to a thaw in their relationship.

A White House official told The Post on Thursday that Trump did not appear upset with Blair and was unlikely to hold him responsible if Republicans were wiped out on Nov. 3. The official described the president’s conversations with Blair as businesslike and focused on campaign tactics.

news.title: Kamala Harris Met With Silence at Mississippi Rally After Quote Flub
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris’ effort to energize voters at a Democratic rally in Mississippi drew a muted response Thursday, as she repeated a convoluted quote inside a high school gym that was far from full.

“You know, I mentor a lot of young people, and I talk to them sometimes and part of the advice I give them is, you know, never let someone else with limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition,” Harris said at the Columbus, Miss., event supporting Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom.

The line received little reaction from the audience, leading Harris to repeat it.

“Let me repeat that: Never let anybody else’s, somebody else’s limited ability to see your capacity to be a limitation on your ambition,” she said, drawing a somewhat stronger response from rally attendees.

FIND OUT MORE: Nassau County Exec Bruce Blakeman Says Hochul-Mamdani Rally Helps Him

“That’s their limitation. That’s not our limitation. That’s their limitation,” Harris added before continuing with another series of remarks.

“We are not limited in our ambition and desire and ability to see what is possible and what can be,” she told the crowd.

Colom, a state district attorney challenging incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) in the midterm elections, acknowledged that his decision to invite the failed 2024 presidential candidate to campaign for him had prompted questions.

“Why would you do that?” Colom said he was asked.

“You know what I told them, ‘Why not?’” the Senate hopeful said before Harris took the stage.

news.title: Hughesy, Karl and co: what happens when celebrities turn political?
news.text:
In recent months, many Australians would have seen or heard celebrities such as Dave Hughes, Karl Stefanovic and Kyle Sandilands becoming more involved in Australia’s political debate.

While it is not new for celebrities to express political opinions, social media has changed how they engage in public debate. 

They can influence people even if they don’t officially endorse a political party or appear at a campaign rally. 

But what is particularly interesting is these personalities are engaging with politics in different ways. 

Capitalising on social grievance

Many Australians are frustrated by cost-of-living pressures, housing affordability and declining trust in political institutions. 

Celebrities often use humour, criticism and relatable commentary to channel those frustrations. 

They position themselves as speaking for ordinary Australians, rather than political elites. Genuine public concerns can be expressed through outrage-driven narratives. 

But this approach can reinforce dissatisfaction rather than encourage informed political debate. For those on the conservative side of the political spectrum who benefit from these engagements, it has been described as “right-wing grifting”.

What are Hughes, Stefanovic and co doing?

Hughes has become increasingly outspoken in his criticism of Labor, focusing on policy and economics. He maintains his political stance is driven by opposition to government mismanagement, rather than opposition to the political left.

He recently attended a Victorian Liberal Party campaign event but stopped his engagement because of concerns it might breach the state’s political donation laws.

Hughes has described himself as a “former lifelong Labor voter”. 

Once one of the highest paid Australian television presenters, Stefanovic has moved further into political commentary through his podcast. 

With guests including political figures and former government officials, he has tackled controversial topics. He recently hosted the conservative CPAC conference in Brisbane. 

Controversial radio host Sandilands is another interesting example, having shifted from his public friendship with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to expressing support for Pauline Hanson and One Nation. 

He claims he even assisted the party with its political messaging, demonstrating how celebrity influence can extend beyond public commentary into political strategy.

More recently, comedian Luke McGregor – who has a degree in economics – has attracted attention for his criticism of the Reserve Bank’s approach to inflation and unemployment. His commentary is more policy-focused than party-politics, demonstrating political influence does not necessarily require an explicit political allegiance.

The changing face of media consumption

These celebrities have all developed relationships with audiences outside politics. Their followers already know their personalities as both celebrities and content creators. 

Audiences understand their humour and may feel a sense of familiarity with them. This creates opportunities to introduce politics into spaces where people might not otherwise actively seek it.

The University of Canberra’s 2026 digital news report highlights how significant the shift towards non-traditional media has become. 

43% of Australian consumers access news from creators and influencers
48% of 18–24 year-olds use TikTok for news
among people consuming influencer-led news, 59% consider it more entertaining, 55% more relatable and 56% easier to understand than traditional news
people who distrust mainstream news tend to view influencers as more trustworthy and authentic than traditional media.

A report from Griffith University and Sentiment Agency, an Australian strategy agency, provides further evidence. 

It examined 564 political creator posts during the 2025 federal election. The findings show creators outpublished traditional media on election and leadership content by four to one on social media. Audiences also identified creators as particularly influential sources of political information. 

The research highlights that while traditional media may be seen by many as more credible, creators connect with audiences. This shapes what people pay attention to, rather than necessarily changing how they vote.

This strategy is not new

Research shows United States president Donald Trump’s media strategy helped him win the so-called first “influencer election” in 2024.

But his engagement with celebrities and content creators is not as simple as podcast appearances or algorithms. Instead, it reflects longstanding relationships with online communities, including those surrounding powerful celebrities such as Joe Rogan and Elon Musk. 

Political influence is more than borrowing a celebrity’s audience. It is about accessing the cultural relationships and credibility they have established. 

It doesn’t always result in election wins, though. The “Kamala is Brat” phenomenon – which emerged after singer Charli XCX called Kamala Harris “brat” following the release of her Brat album – shows how celebrities, memes and popular culture can make politicians more relevant to younger audiences.

It comes with risk

Political commentary can alienate existing audiences. People may enjoy someone’s comedy or television appearances without necessarily trusting their political judgement.

There are other grey areas too. As political commentary increasingly occurs outside traditional journalism, celebrities and creators do not operate under the same editorial expectations around accuracy, verification and balance. 

Ultimately, the greatest influence of these celebrities may not be changing individual votes. It is likely in shaping the conversations that precede them. They influence which issues dominate attention, how audiences perceive political leaders, and whose explanations they find credible.

In an increasingly fragmented media environment, that is actually a significant form of political power.
news.summary: Celebrities may not directly sway people’s votes but they do shape conversations in the media. That is a significant form of political power.

news.title: 'Total Disgrace' Trump Demands Lebron James Apologise After He Practises Golf Swing During National Anthem
news.text: Donald Trump has called LeBron James a 'TOTAL DISGRACE' and demanded an apology after footage showed the NBA star miming a golf swing during the US national anthem. The president accused James of disrespecting the country and Americans who died for its flag.The footage came from the Philadelphia 76ers' season opener against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday, 20 October. Trump responded on Truth Social on Thursday, adding to criticism of the player's movements during the performance.Neither James nor the 76ers had publicly responded to Trump's remarks at the time of publication.Trump Demands Apology to Fallen American Heroes'While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country!' Trump wrote. 'I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE.'He demanded that James 'apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!'The president's post followed online criticism of the footage, which showed James moving while his teammates stood alongside him during the anthem.What the LeBron James Footage ShowsJames appeared to swing an imaginary golf club and practise his shooting form as singer Avery Wilson performed the anthem. He was not holding a golf club.Yardbarker's account also described him stretching and practising his free-throw form. Most of his teammates remained still during the performance.The pre-game sequence followed the Knicks' championship ring and banner ceremony. For James, it preceded his first regular-season appearance with Philadelphia and the start of his NBA-record 24th season.James's Philadelphia Debut Ends in VictoryThe 76ers spoiled New York's championship celebrations with a 106–100 victory. Tyrese Maxey led Philadelphia with 28 points, while fellow new arrival Jaylen Brown added 19.James finished with 14 points, nine rebounds and seven assists as he began his latest chapter alongside Brown, Maxey and Joel Embiid.His post-game comments focused on finding his rhythm with his new teammates.'I could be a lot better,' James told NBC. 'Still getting my rhythm, obviously just a little bit over two weeks with the new squad. But I like the way we played.'The victory gave Philadelphia a winning start against the defending champions, while the anthem footage drew attention away from James's on-court debut.Trump and James Have Clashed BeforeJames's disagreements with Trump stretch back years and have included White House invitations, race and presidential elections.In 2017, James called Trump a 'bum' after the president withdrew a White House invitation to the Golden State Warriors following Stephen Curry's indication that he did not want to attend.'Going to White House was a great honor until you showed up!' James wrote.The following year, Trump questioned James's intelligence after an interview with CNN's Don Lemon in which the player accused him of using sport to divide Americans.Trump ended his post with 'I like Mike!'—an apparent reference to Michael Jordan. Jordan subsequently said through a spokesperson: 'I support LeBron James. He's doing an amazing job for his community.'James also endorsed Kamala Harris against Trump in the 2024 presidential election.'When I think about my kids and my family and how they will grow up, the choice is clear to me,' he wrote, followed by 'VOTE KAMALA HARRIS!!!

news.title: At the Races: Family in the fray
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Daniela Altimari, Niels Lesniewski and Mary Ellen McIntire

An ad produced by Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, features the mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent, calling her daughter a liar and urging voters to reject her.

The ad doesn’t mention that Acton has long been estranged from her mother over allegations that her stepfather sexually abused her, which led to him being charged with rape when Acton was 12, according to court documents obtained by the National Review. He was indicted by a grand jury but fled town and was never tried. Throughout her career in public life, Acton has spoken about the abuse.

The spot drew widespread condemnation from people across the political spectrum, including from Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” DeWine told reporters Thursday.

But the ad drew high-profile defenders from the White House. Vice President JD Vance said he was “disgusted” by Republicans who criticized the spot. President Donald Trump praised Ramaswamy and urged him not to take the ad down. “The Press is trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt,’” Trump wrote on social media Thursday.

It wasn’t the only attack ad using a candidate's family to hit the airwaves this week. In Maine’s high-profile Senate race, a top Senate Republican super PAC launched a radio spot labeling Democrat Troy Jackson as a “freak” who has “two kids with his cousin” over a jaunty country jingle.

Jackson’s Republican opponent, Sen. Susan Collins, is among those calling for the ad to be removed.

The midterm election cycle has seen a spike in ads aimed at politicians’ families. In Iowa, a Democratic super PAC produced an ad accusing Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, and her husband of blurring ethical lines. Republicans lobbed a similar line of attack against the husband of Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who is running for Senate in New Hampshire.

But critics say the Acton ad represents a new low, and one notable Ohio Republican predicts the spot will backfire on Ramaswamy.

“[The] floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor,’’ former Rep. James B. Renacci, the 2018 GOP nominee for Senate, posted on X. “And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well.”

Starting gate

Tar Heel State tightrope: In the race for North Carolina’s open Senate seat, Republican Michael Whatley has consistently trailed in the polls behind Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s battle-tested former governor. Now, with time running out and national party funding drying up, Whatley faces a high-stakes balancing act: winning over unaffiliated voters who have soured on Trump without alienating a Republican base that remains fiercely loyal to the president.

#NC01: North Carolina Republicans are counting on the new congressional map to help retired Army Col. Laurie Buckhout defy the current political headwinds in her rematch against Democratic Rep. Don Davis. But Trump’s sinking poll numbers have scrambled the calculus and turned what was meant to be a likely Republican flip into a Toss-up race.

Spotlight on Virginia: Republicans are defending a trio of seats in Virginia that highlight the range of districts that have made it onto the House battleground this year. Rep. Jen Kiggans is used to tough races in her swingy district, while neighboring Rep. Rob Wittman faces a competitive reelection for the first time. Democrats are also targeting Rep. John McGuire’s seat, which Trump carried by 12 points two years ago. 

Q3 roundup: Democrats have expanded the Senate and House battlegrounds in this year’s midterm elections, and new federal fundraising filings show their candidates largely outraised their Republican opponents in the third quarter. On the Senate side, that included Democrats in deep-red states such as Kansas and South Carolina. House Democratic candidates in targeted districts also reported raising big sums as they try to keep pace with the massive spending by GOP outside groups. But Republican incumbents in most of these races entered October with more cash on hand. 

#SCSEN: Trump traveled to South Carolina this week to boost appointed Sen. Darline Graham, who, our colleague Savannah Behrmann writes, is locked in an unexpectedly tight race against Democrat Annie Andrews.

E15 boon: Trump said at a rally in Kansas this week that he would only make permanent the year-round use of a fuel blend containing a higher percentage of ethanol if Republicans hold the state’s Senate seat, as Niels reported with colleague David Jordan. “With Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year-round E15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it,” the president said. 

Fight for the heartland: The high cost of diesel is underscoring tight Senate races in Iowa and Kansas, two red states where some farmers are considering voting for Democrats this year, Savannah, David and our colleague Ryan Kelly report. 

Data center attacks: Democrats running for Senate are pressing their opponents in debates and ads about artificial intelligence data center policy, often as a proxy for voter fears about the economy and local impacts, our colleague Allison Mollenkamp writes.

Carolina in our minds: Campaigns in both North and South Carolina are ramping up and Roll Call photojournalist Bill Clark was on the trail with Daniela, following candidates in Eastern North Carolina and in the Charleston, S.C., area. He also spoke about the experience in a video for Roll Call’s Capitol Lens.

Growing coalition: The New Democrat Coalition, already the largest ideological bloc within the House Democratic Caucus with more than 100 members, is poised to grow bigger and more influential next year, Arizona Rep. Greg Stanton, who chairs the group’s campaign arm, said in an interview with Roll Call’s Nina Heller.

Virginia Democrat arrested: L. Louise Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate who led Democrats’ court-blocked redistricting push in the commonwealth this year, was charged Thursday with leading a “criminal marijuana distribution enterprise.” Lucas, who surrendered to authorities, according to the Justice Department, struck a defiant note in a statement, saying, ”I will not be intimidated. I will not be bullied. And I will not back down."

Oliver out: Shawn Oliver, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor in Massachusetts, suspended his campaign after he was arrested on drunken driving charges following a car crash. The Republican ticket, led by businessman Mike Minogue, faces an uphill climb in the Bay State, where Democratic Gov. Maura Healey is heavily favored to win a second term.

Democrats spending where? Senate Majority PAC launched a $1.2 million ad campaign in Mississippi to boost prosecutor Scott Colom’s challenge to Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a notable entrance in a state that Trump won by 24 points in 2024.

Fabricated polls: An upstart group calling itself Wedgewood Polling has admitted that almost all of its work product was faked, including polling that Michigan Democrat Mallory McMorrow suggested had contributed to the premature end to her Senate campaign. The firm copped up to the bogus polls following an investigation by FiftyPlusOne.

Amodei votes third party: Retiring Republican Rep. Mark Amodei told Politico that he didn’t vote for David Flippo, the GOP nominee to succeed him in Nevada’s 2nd District, opting instead for independent Lynn Chapman. The publication had previously reported on Amodei’s concerns with Flippo, who switched to the 2nd District from the 4th after it became open. With Democrats targeting the red-leaning district, Axios reported that the DCCC has posted messaging suggesting outside group ads should promote Chapman as an option for Republican female voters.

Ad watch: The Human Rights Campaign Equality Votes PAC announced a $1 million ad campaign to support California state Sen. Scott Wiener, who is running to succeed Nancy Pelosi. The former speaker is backing San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, a move Wiener allies say is driven primarily by a personal vendetta, The Washington Post reports.

Stepping back: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee said it would stop issuing endorsements and contributing directly to candidates, although its super PAC, the United Democracy Project, plans to continue. The decision comes as support from AIPAC became something of a liability in certain Democratic primary contests this year.

Bloomberg’s millions: Former New York Mayor Mike Bloomberg has sent Democrats about $80 million for the midterm elections, at least $50 million of which is going to support House candidates, The New York Times reports. 

Maxxlooking: At rallies across the nation, Trump has devoted time to an unusual topic for a political event: men’s bodies. As The New York Times reports, the president has recently praised the appearance of House hopeful Ed Gallrein of Kentucky, called Georgia Rep. Mike Collins a “good-looking man” and marveled at Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s physique.

Nathan's notes

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales made 30 race rating changes last week, all in Democrats’ favor. “Republicans are running out of time to change the trajectory of the midterms,” writes Nathan.

Among the notable Senate updates were Kansas moving from Likely Republican to Tilt Republican and Florida entering the battleground, going from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. 

On the House side, several races in deep-red territory are now rated competitive (Likely Republican), including Wyoming’s at-large district, Arkansas’ 2nd, Indiana’s 5th and Nebraska’s 1st. 

What we're reading

Leading from the middle: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani was elected as a democratic socialist but is governing as a moderate, asserts this commentary piece from The Atlantic.

Looming battle: “Protect women’s sports” has become a campaign slogan for Republicans running against transgender rights. But as Politico reports, there’s a split emerging among conservatives as some push for a broad rethinking of Title IX, the federal law barring sex discrimination that’s driven the growth in women’s sports. 

#MESEN: Roll Call alumna Bridget Bowman, now of NBC News, reported from Lewiston, Maine, a city that has been shifting to the right in recent elections, but where voters could be reconsidering their votes in a way that could affect Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection bid. 

Quietly trying to make history: New Hampshire Rep. Chris Pappas would be the first openly gay male senator if he wins his state’s open seat next month, but as The New York Times reports, that hasn’t been a focal point of his campaign.

The count: 64

That's the number of House races that three of Trump's political groups have directly spent on so far during the general election.

The three committees — MAGA Inc., No Going Back PAC and Safety & Affordability PAC — spent a combined $110.3 million through last week on the 64 races, according to a Roll Call analysis of new federal filings.

Most of the money — $59.8 million covering ads, mail pieces and text message campaigns — was earmarked for 41 Republican-held districts. According to the latest ratings by Inside Elections, Republicans are currently favored to retain 21 of them, while Trump carried 37 of the 41 two years ago, by an average of 8.7 points. 

While the spending skews defensive overall, the top targets between the three groups are two Florida districts that were expressly redrawn to give Republicans the advantage. Nearly $8 million has been spent on Florida’s 25th District, held by Democrat Jared Moskowitz, and $6.7 million has been allocated to the 14th District, represented by Rep. Kathy Castor. Inside Elections rates both races as Toss-ups. 

The three committees have so far spent a combined $50.7 million dollars on the 18 Toss-up races, according to Inside Elections: six seats currently held by Democrats ($4.3 million per seat) and 12 being defended by the GOP ($2.1 million per race). 

– by Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #NY17

Candidates: Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces a tough reelection fight against Democrat Cait Conley, an Army veteran who worked as a national security official in the Biden administration. 

Why it matters: New York’s 17th District is one of a handful of Republican-held House seats that Kamala Harris carried in 2024, making it a top battleground. Lawler has been a top Democratic target since his first election in 2022, when he ousted DCCC Chair Sean Patrick Maloney. 

Cash dash: Both Lawler and Conley have proved to be strong fundraisers. The Republican closed September with $2.9 million on hand, while Conley had $1.1 million banked for the campaign’s final stretch. Outside groups have spent more than $13 million on the race so far. The Congressional Leadership Fund, House Republicans’ top super PAC, spent $6.5 million attacking Conley through Oct. 20, while its Democratic counterpart, House Majority PAC, spent $1.1 million opposing Lawler. Elon Musk’s America PAC dropped $548,000 on Lawler’s behalf, while the Trump-aligned No Going Back PAC spent $275,000. The environmental groups EDF Action Votes and LCV Victory Fund collectively invested more than $1.3 million in support of Conley.

Backers: Lawler has touted endorsements from several labor groups and also picked up support from retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine. Conley counts on support from several veterans groups such as VoteVets and New Politics and Democratic outfits such as EMILY’s List, DMFI PAC and Majority Democrats. 

What they’re saying: In a district that Trump narrowly lost, Lawler has sought to emphasize his willingness to work across the aisle and go toe-to-toe with the president. On air, he has highlighted his efforts last year to raise the SALT tax deduction cap in Republicans’ massive tax and spending law. In a recent ad, he pointed out that Conley doesn’t own a home in the district. Conley has emphasized her military service, which included serving six tours overseas. In an ad made in coordination with the DCCC, she tied the conflict in Iran to higher costs and criticized Lawler for voting against measures aimed at ending the war. 

Terrain: The 17th District is a suburban stronghold in the Lower Hudson Valley and includes portions of Westchester County, just north of New York City, and all of Rockland and Putnam counties. Harris carried the seat by less than a point in 2024, while Lawler won a second term by about 6 points. Inside Elections rates the race a Toss-up.

Candidates’ final fundraising reports before the election are due before Friday with the Federal Election Commission. The pre-general election filings cover the first 14 days of October.

Meanwhile, Trump’s barnstorming through red America continues, with an appearance Thursday evening in Iowa, followed by Florida on Friday and Georgia on Saturday. The president will be back on the road next week with scheduled trips to Mississippi on Monday, Texas on Tuesday and Ohio on Wednesday.

news.title: Senate Republicans’ Top PAC Dropping $1 Million Into Deep-Red Mississippi
news.text:
Senate Republicans’ top campaign arm planned to spend $1 million in deep-red Mississippi Thursday after the Senate race became unusually competitive, a source familiar confirmed to the Daily Caller News Foundation. 

The Senate Leadership Fund planned to launch an advertisement campaign in “the low seven figures” to support Republican Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who leads Democratic Mississippi Senate nominee Scott Colom by single digits, Semafor first reported. The decision came after Senate Democrats’ top campaign arm planned to spend $1.2 million on television advertisements to boost Colom. (RELATED: Republicans Are Even Ramping Up Campaign Spending In Deep-Red South Dakota Now)

NEW — Senate Leadership Fund plans to spend more than $1 million in Mississippi’s Senate race to defend Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith against Democrat Scott Colom, per Semafor. The buy follows Senate Majority PAC’s $1.2 million ad campaign.— VoteHub (@VoteHub) October 22, 2026

A Data for Progress survey from August found Hyde-Smith in the lead by six points, while an Impact Research survey from April found her leading by three points, according to The New York Times. 

Wedgewood Polls admitted to fabricating a poll suggesting that Hyde-Smith held a four-point lead. It said that the surveys were part of an “experimental project” to expose how easily a fabricated polling firm could mislead the public.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris traveled to Mississippi Thursday to campaign with Colom. Democratic Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Democratic Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson and former President Barack Obama campaigned and endorsed Colom. Obama appeared in a commercial to endorse the Mississippi Democrat. 

President Donald Trump won Mississippi by a 24-point margin against Harris. The state has not had a Democratic U.S. senator since former Democratic Mississippi Sen. John Stennis retired in 1989. 

Hyde-Smith won her 2020 election by a 54.1% to 44.1% margin. 

Republican PACs spent unprecedented amounts to defend Republican-held seats, including in Texas and Kansas. Republicans spent over $300 million to support Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, $14 million to support Republican Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall and $5 million to support Republican South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham. 

The PACs scaled back their time and resources in North Carolina and Georgia, two battleground states. Democrats also slashed ad spending in the states while Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Democratic North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper held comfortable leads in the polls.

news.title: Kamala Harris Stumps in Mississippi as GOP Moves to Protect Senate Seat
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is campaigning in Mississippi on Thursday for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom, as Republicans face an unexpectedly competitive contest in a state President Donald Trump won by nearly 23 points in 2024. Harris is scheduled to rally with Colom in Columbus on Thursday evening, following a rural-healthcare roundtable in Clarksdale. Her visit comes just four days before Trump is due to travel to Mississippi to campaign for incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith at a rally in Corinth, underscoring the unusual national attention being devoted to a Senate race in one of the country’s most reliably Republican states. Hyde-Smith campaign manager Jake Monssen told Newsweek on Thursday that Trump had offered to help the senator “rally voters and support her get-out-the-vote efforts.” He rejected suggestions that the visit reflected vulnerability. “We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith to the U.S. Senate,” Monssen said. Newsweek reached out on Thursday to the Colom campaign for comment. Why Republicans Are Moving to Protect the Mississippi Senate Seat Mississippi would ordinarily be an unlikely Senate battleground. Trump carried the state with 60.9 percent of the vote in 2024, compared with 38 percent for Harris, and Republicans have the seat for decades. Axios reported Wednesday that the Senate Leadership Fund, which is aligned with Republican Senate leadership, had reviewed Mississippi two weeks earlier and concluded that spending was not necessary but is now reassessing the contest and may spend to protect Hyde-Smith. The Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC announced Tuesday that it was spending an initial $1.2 million on television statewide through Election Day, November 3, along with a digital campaign. Senate Majority PAC spokesperson Lauren French told Newsweek on Thursday that the $1.2 million campaign would run statewide through Election Day and that the group would “keep watching this race closely for further investments.” The investment marked a change in strategy after Democrats previously said their resources were stretched too thin across an expanding Senate map to spend in Mississippi, Politico reported Tuesday. Senators Raphael Warnock of Georgia and Ruben Gallego of Arizona had pushed for more investment in the contest, while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York had pitched donors on Mississippi and hosted a fundraiser for Colom earlier this year. French said that Trump’s planned visit was evidence of how competitive Democrats believe the race has become. “When Donald Trump has to fly into a state he carried by more than 20 points to prop up an incumbent Republican eight days before Election Day, that tells you where this race stands,” French said. Colom campaign manager Gerard Henderson pointed to the investment as evidence of the campaign’s momentum. “Mississippi is in play because thousands of Mississippians volunteered and chipped in to make this race competitive,” he said in a statement to Politico on Tuesday. “We clearly have the momentum and resources to win on November 3rd and prove to the nation that Mississippi Matters.” What Mississippi Senate Polls Show About Hyde-Smith vs. Colom A Data for Progress survey conducted August 5-15 found Hyde-Smith ahead of Colom by 6 points, 44 percent to 38 percent, with independent candidate Ty Pinkins at 7 percent. The survey of 1,018 likely voters was sponsored by the Democratic-aligned Way to Lead PAC, Democracy Alliance and Democracy Strategy Partners. Prediction market Kalshi, meanwhile, gave Hyde-Smith a 90.3 percent chance of winning as of Thursday afternoon, compared with 9.7 percent for Colom. The late spending and visits by national political figures provide separate evidence that both parties are paying closer attention to the contest but do not show that Hyde-Smith is likely to lose. Why Kamala Harris Is Campaigning for Scott Colom Harris is the latest in a series of nationally known Democrats to get behind Colom. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Colom in an ad that began running this week. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is scheduled to campaign for him along the Mississippi Gulf Coast on October 27. Senators Cory Booker of New Jersey, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland have already visited Mississippi to support Colom, while Warnock has also campaigned on his behalf. Hyde-Smith has attacked her opponent over his ties to national Democrats and the prominent party figures campaigning on his behalf. Colom has countered by portraying Hyde-Smith as out of touch with Mississippi voters and criticizing her for not debating him. Monssen told Newsweek on Thursday that the Harris visit showed Colom was “beholden to the far left,” while blaming the Biden-Harris administration for inflation and problems at the southern border. Donald Trump Heads to Mississippi to Help Cindy Hyde-Smith Republicans are bringing in their own biggest political draw. Trump's Corinth rally is scheduled for October 26, eight days before Election Day. That puts the two candidates from the 2024 presidential election on opposing sides of the Mississippi Senate contest within days of each other. Trump has backed Hyde-Smith since well before the race began attracting heightened national attention. In March 2025, he described her as “100 percent MAGA” and gave her his “Complete and Total Endorsement” for reelection. Could Democrats Really Flip a Senate Seat in Mississippi? Democrats face a formidable electoral history. No Democrat has won a Mississippi Senate election since John C. Stennis in 1982, and the party last won a statewide race in 2015. Trump carried Mississippi by approximately 23 points in 2024, while Republicans control the governorship and both chambers of the state Legislature. Hyde-Smith, however, has never received more than 55 percent of the vote in either of her previous Senate victories. She defeated Democrat Mike Espy by about 10 points in 2020 after beating him by less than 8 points in the 2018 special-election runoff. There have also been signs of Democratic competitiveness below the presidential level. Republican Governor Tate Reeves defeated Democrat Brandon Presley by about 3 points in 2023. Democrats gained two Mississippi state Senate seats in special elections in November 2025, breaking the Republican supermajority in the chamber. Those contests followed court-ordered redistricting that created additional majority-Black districts, however, making them substantially different from this year’s statewide Senate race. Mississippi also has the highest proportion of Black residents of any state, giving Democrats a substantial base of support while leaving them dependent on strong turnout and gains elsewhere in the electorate to win statewide. The question now is whether Colom can translate the favorable national environment for Democrats, late financial investment and support from prominent national Democrats into something much more difficult: a statewide Democratic victory in a deep-red state. news.summary: Kamala Harris campaigns for Scott Colom as GOP attention turns to Mississippi’s unexpectedly competitive Senate race.

news.title: Trump Faces a Midterm Crisis in Kansas After 100 Years
news.text:
George McGill’s unassuming grave sits on an exposed Kansas prairie, close to the geographic center of the contiguous United States.

Past the neat, compact cemetery, fields of corn and stretches of wild grass run uninterrupted toward the horizon. A weather-beaten barn is the only visible structure. Visitors are rare, and even Kansans—known for their long memories—have largely forgotten McGill’s name.

McGill was the last Democrat elected to the US Senate from this deeply Republican state. That victory came in 1932, amid the Great Depression, as drought and dust transformed the plains. Since then, Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Kansas for 94 years—the longest uninterrupted run for any party in any state in American history.

Yet that historic streak could end in the midterm elections on November 3. Donald Trump carried Kansas by landslides three times, but the average of the polls now shows the Senate contest tied.

A Democratic win could also give the party the final boost needed to take control of the US Senate, currently held by Republicans 53 seats to 47. That would set up a punishing final two years for Trump, including the prospect of impeachment. With Republicans expected to lose the House, retaining the Senate has become their central priority.

The growing number of Kansans willing to consider a Democrat is clear about whom they blame for the unexpected vulnerability: Trump. His approval rating in the state has fallen to 40 percent.

In Pawnee Rock, the hamlet of just 180 residents where McGill was raised, staunchly Republican Mayor Paul Umble has no plans to change parties. Even so, he concedes with a wry smile: “I’m not thrilled with Trump at the moment.”

The reason is easy to understand. In Kansas, the election’s defining issue can be summed up in one phrase: the cost of diesel. In a state roughly the combined size of England and Scotland, goods and farm products depend heavily on rail and diesel-powered trucks.

At the Pawnee Rock gas station, the diesel price has climbed to $6.09, which locals attribute to Trump’s Iran war. Before Iran, the price was about $4. The timing is especially painful because farmers are in the middle of harvest. “There’s a lot of upset about it,” Umble says. “People are struggling.”

Republicans are still expected to dominate rural western Kansas on November 3—a region where, as the saying goes, even the Wicked Witch of the West could win with a red ribbon. Democrats, meanwhile, should build a substantial advantage in the suburbs around Kansas City. That leaves Sedgwick County, positioned near the state’s geographic and political center, as the likely battleground that could determine both the Kansas result and control of the Senate.

Sedgwick County includes Wichita, a city of about 400,000 on the muddy Arkansas River, watched over by the famous Native American statue known as the Keeper of the Plains. Trump defeated Kamala Harris there in 2024 by 56 percent to 42 percent, close to his 16-point statewide margin. Democrats must improve significantly in the county if they are to win.

The two Senate candidates are both gray-haired men in their 60s, and from a distance their images on campaign billboards can look remarkably alike. Both, however, carry political baggage.

Democrat Adam Hamilton is the more naturally charismatic of the two. He leads the state’s largest megachurch, a sleek modern building that resembles a UFO that has landed. On the campaign trail, he frequently invokes The Wizard of Oz, arguing that Washington lacks the brain, heart and courage represented by the tin man, scarecrow and lion. But Hamilton is also contending with a scandal involving allegations that his church covered up sexual abuse.

Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, an OB-GYN, faces controversies of his own, including questions over lawsuits brought against his patients and allegations that he effectively lived in Florida.

As criticism mounted over lawsuits seeking payment for medical bills, Marshall said he had not personally taken part in the cases, describing them as routine collection efforts.

He has explained that his Florida home allowed him to spend time with his grandchildren. Claims that he spent too much time there, he said, were “all lies” and a “myth made by the social media Nazis.”

At the rally, Trump made an unsubstantiated claim of his own, saying Marshall would be “breaking the law” if he failed to collect money patients owed.

However, as a staunch loyalist, Marshall’s biggest hurdle to winning over independents in Wichita, is his links to Trump.

As early voting began at Wichita’s main library, truck driver Greg Florence, 65, a former Republican, told Our News Outlet: ‘I just think the Republican Party have basically sold their soul to the devil. Everything they’re doing to go along with Donald Trump. I don’t like it.

‘It (diesel) is freaking ridiculously high. I never seen it that high. We’re just never ending the (Iran) war. Who’s to blame? Donald Trump. He’s the president.’

Jeff Mohr, 65, a retired accountant, said he had voted Republican most of his life, but was going Democrat.

‘Mostly, it’s Trump’s demeanor,’ he said. ‘And the Republicans won’t stand their ground. I want checks from Congress on the Defense Secretary and DHS (Department of Homeland Security).’

Lynn Ferguson, 62, a registered Republican who works in a quilt shop, said she was now ‘leaning Democrat’ because Marshall backed Trump over the January 6 riot.

‘I think integrity is a big issue,’ she said. ‘I just feel like anybody that is an election denier does not deserve to be in office.’

Rising grocery prices, and her children being unable to find affordable housing, were factors, but her shift was more about ‘who we are’ as a nation, she said. 

She was appalled by recent ICE raids in southwest Kansas, which saw over 100 arrests and hurt the beef and dairy industries as Hispanic workers stayed home.

‘You know, engraved on the base of the Statue of Liberty is the poem, “Give me your tired, your poor, those yearning to be free…” we’re a country of immigrants,’ said Ferguson.

More than one voter invoked the spirit of John Brown, the abolitionist who took up arms against slavery in Kansas

Damien Gilbert 32, a Democrat, said his father, a lifelong Republican, had joined him out canvassing for Hamilton. For his father, the main issue was Ukraine.

‘This (Kansas) was the home of [Former President] Dwight D Eisenhower,’ Gilbert said. ‘The thing that’s really got him (my father) angry is what Trump has done with our relationship to our allies and especially his betrayal of Ukraine. We are paying attention. We’re disgusted.

‘Kansans are, by and large, decent, normal, commonsense folks. We also don’t appreciate feeling taken for granted.’

It’s that kind of sentiment that led Trump to fly to Wichita this week to turn things around. And he had some explaining to do.

In addition to the Iran war-induced diesel spike, Trump recently signed a declaration allowing cheap beef imports into the US in a bid to reduce the price of hamburgers. But in Kansas, where cows outnumber people two to one, ranchers were outraged at being undercut.

Last month, the President also announced Canadian plane maker Bombardier would be banned from selling jets in the US. Bombardier is a major employer in Wichita, which is known as the ‘Air Capital of the World.’

It all amounted to a self-inflicted Trump triple whammy – on diesel, beef and planes – against one the states that has been most loyal to him, backing him with huge margins in three presidential elections.

NEXT UP: Feds Charge 15 in $1.8B Southern California Medical Fraud Sweep

However, when he arrived at the 6,000-capacity Heartland Credit Union Arena just outside Wichita on Monday night, all appeared forgiven, at least by the MAGA base. A huge crowd featuring women in bedazzled Trump jackets and men in cowboy hats snaked through a field among trucks bearing the slogan ‘EAT BEEF.’

Michael Green, 66, dressed head to toe in stars and stripes, was in line eight hours early. Looking at the thousands-strong army behind him, he said: ‘I would like to think the silent majority, in this case, is a conservative Republican, will win this for Roger Marshall.

‘In my opinion, most conservatives are nose to the grindstone; they work every day, earn a living, take care of their family, treat everybody fair. They’re not in everybody’s face.’

Doug Hye, 72, a retired ‘technology guy,’ said he was ‘absolutely sure’ Wichita would decide the result.

‘I think this (rally) will get out the vote,’ he said. ‘A lot of the independents in Kansas are really Republicans but they kind of want to hold the Republicans accountable. So, they just say they’re an independent.’

Jenny Zeller, 50, a hairdresser, said: ‘Everybody needs to quit worrying about the price of gas. It has nothing to do with Trump, nothing to do with this election.’

Shirley Rainey, 57, a grandmother, said of a Democrat potentially getting elected: ‘It just scares me to even think about it, honestly. So I just pray people get out and vote. I’ve heard his (Hamilton’s) church is either divided, or broke apart, I’m not sure which.’

Outside the rally, protesters held up ‘Trump is a traitor’ signs but, this being Kansas, one of them sincerely wished passing Trump supporters a good night.

Inside the arena, a giant screen declared ‘God Made Trump’ and Marshall came dancing on stage, fist-pumping to Johnny B. Goode, before claiming his ‘woke’ opponent ‘doesn’t know the difference between a bull and a steer,’ ‘supports drag shows,’ believes people ‘shouldn’t drive trucks,’ and, worst of all, ‘wants Kansans to stop eating beef!’

Then, he brought on legendary rocker and hunter Ted Nugent, who told the whooping crowd: ‘I bowl with a 10mm (handgun)! This is the heartland! You ARE the heartland! They’re not Democrats… they’re communists!’

When the President took the stage, it was vintage 2016 Trump. He free-wheeled for an hour and 40 minutes, during which he accused Hamilton of ‘mocking Jesus’ and being ‘very strange.’ For good measure, the President suggested that Hamilton may be a ‘pervert.’

The biggest crowd response of the night came when he accused ‘Dumocrats’ of wanting ‘transgender for everybody and the absolute mutilization of your children.’

Trump also revealed that he hadn’t known Bombardier had a base in Wichita and would ‘take care’ of the workers there. He also vowed to launch a ‘harvest fuel relief program’ providing farmers $8 billion to offset diesel costs.

While some Kansas ranchers have criticized Trump over the cheap beef imports, others see it as a blip and media hype rather than a genuine issue.

North of Wichita, on his idyllic farm amid some of his 100 head of Angus cows, rancher Brad Rayl, a Republican, shook his head and said: ‘Everybody lost their mind, it moved the cattle market for a day. It was a non-event.’

He said people looking at the business case over many years knew there was only one choice in the election, but people in rural areas had to actually get out and vote.

‘I think he (Marshall) wins by a nose,’ he said.

In 2020 Marshall won Kansas by 11 points, and Sedgwick County by nine points.

Across Kansas, 45 per cent of the roughly 2 million voters are registered Republicans, 25 percent registered Democrats and 30 percent unaffiliated. The state is being heavily polled and is essentially a dead heat. An Emerson College poll from last month showed Hamilton winning the independents by 15 points.

A colossal amount of money is pouring into the race with nearly $60 million spent so far. For the final straight, Republicans have bought $10 million worth of TV ads, and Democrats $5 million.

The ads are an unabashedly cynical and negative race to the bottom by both sides.

Republicans are focusing on Hamilton’s handling of an incident involving a volunteer accused of molesting two teenage boys at a camp connected to his Church of the Resurrection, which is the nation’s largest United Methodist Church congregation.

The allegations were only investigated internally, the volunteer returned to the camp and was ⁠again accused of inappropriate behavior before eventually being reported to police. Hamilton has admitted the church should have gone to police sooner but denies a cover-up.

Republicans ran a TV advert accusing him of ‘protecting a pedophile.’ Democrats responded with an ad accusing Marshall of ‘protecting child abusers and rapists’ because he voted against releasing the Epstein Files.

They have also targeted him for having a large home in Sarasota, Florida home while his residence in Kansas is a 1,120sq ft cabin on a ranch north of Wichita. Amid the allegations of sunning himself, Marshall sold the Florida home for $1.35 million last week.

Coincidentally, his Kansas cabin is close to Pawnee Rock. Mayor Umble told Our News Outlet that Marshall had spent a lot of time in the area and worked at a nearby hospital.

‘He delivered a lot of babies,’ Mayor Umble said.

Meanwhile, Republican strategists are pouring into the state as part of a bid to rescue Marshall. They know many Republicans are mad but believe they will come home on Election Day. However, no one is staking their hunting cabin on it.

Dr Alexandra Middlewood, associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, told Our News Outlet that voters in the state were treating the midterms as a referendum on Trump.

‘Particularly the diesel issue here in Kansas is really impacting and a lot of voters are able to make that direct connection to the war in Iran, which the president has started,’ she said. ‘And Roger Marshall has tied himself very, very closely to the President.’

For Marshall, it is a balancing act. He must hope that Trump’s supporters turn out en masse for him, while also trying not to alienate independents.

‘He is really between a rock and a hard place,’ said Middlewood. ‘To be honest, having this rally here, just north of Wichita, is going to hurt Roger Marshall just as much as it may help him. A lot of voters are feeling betrayed by the President.

‘It’s really this perfect storm of issues in the United States right now that have to do with the economy, but also the (Democratic) candidate for Senate is more moderate, is already incredibly well known in the state, he’s the pastor of the largest church and people know who he is.

‘It (a Democratic win) would be a wake up call to the Republican Party. The loss of a Senate seat in Kansas, one that has been held by a Republican for nearly 100 years, would be a large crack in the Republican armor, and a sure sign that the Republican Party is in major trouble, and not just here in Kansas.’

news.title: Supreme Court Justice Kagan warns some conservative rulings have been 'destructive of our democracy'
news.text: Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan suggested Tuesday that some recent decisions by her conservative colleagues have undermined democracy, while admitting at times they had also pushed back against the Trump administration. Kagan took part in a discussion on recent U.S. Supreme Court decisions while speaking at Catholic University's Columbus School of Law. She specifically took issue with cases like Louisiana v. Callais, which ruled in a 6-3 decision that race-based gerrymandering of congressional districts was unconstitutional. In her dissent, Kagan called the decision the "latest chapter in the majority's now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act" and she continued to criticize election and campaign finance decisions made by the court. KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS "Part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a kind of lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions," Kagan said, according to NBC News. She went on to warn that decisions that undermined voters' ability to choose their candidates were "very destructive of our democracy." "I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn't work as well as it should," Kagan said. SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES She also criticized the conservative view of originalism in the Supreme Court, calling it "misconceived" and "not a very good match with the Constitution we have." Kagan claimed that these and other decisions have contributed to the country becoming more "polarized," particularly around campaign finance. "I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they're right," she said. CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION However, Kagan stopped short of accusing the court of being beholden to President Donald Trump, pointing out several cases where even conservative justices "definitely pushed back" on his agenda. Trump nominated three of the current justices on the court in Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett. In a comment to Fox News Digital, Heritage Foundation Senior Legal Fellow of Courts and the Constitution Zack Smith denounced Kagan and what he characterized as far-left politicians' efforts to delegitimize SCOTUS decisions. "The job of the Court is not to play politics with its decisions. Instead, its job is to faithfully apply the Constitution and other laws as they are written. Justice Kagan has disagreed with the majority of her colleagues in some of those decisions, but that doesn't mean they are illegitimate or even wrongly decided," Smith said. news.title: RILEY GAINES: Call Her Daddy's advice is a dangerous recipe for lifelong regret
news.text: In a viral exchange this week, Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper and actress Sophia Bush offered young women a familiar piece of relationship advice: If you're questioning whether to leave your marriage because you fear you won't find someone better, the answer is always yes. Bush went further, suggesting that the fear of being too old or unreasonable for wanting more is a product of the patriarchy. Cooper built her brand largely by celebrating sexual experimentation, including encouraging young women to engage in highly explicit sexual experimentation early in dating. This is the same podcast Kamala Harris joined prior to the 2024 election, but I digress. RILEY GAINES FIRES BACK AT ALEX COOPER’S GRAPHIC DATING ADVICE: ‘IT IS NOT EMPOWERMENT. IT IS POISON’ Bush is now on her third marriage, with the first one lasting 5 months, the second lasting about a year, and the third to a woman. These are the voices our culture elevates as influential guides for young women. But enough about the who. Let's examine the what. The exchange reveals a worldview in which something better is always waiting. That personal and fleeting dissatisfaction is sufficient reason to abandon a commitment, and that the pursuit of more is interchangeable with empowerment. More what, exactly? More excitement? More affirmation? More freedom? Another relationship that will inevitably encounter the same imperfections as the last? At what point do we consider whether the relentless pursuit of more is precisely what leaves us feeling we have less? AMERICAN WOMEN HAVE BEEN LIED TO ABOUT MOTHERHOOD AND IT’S TIME TO FIX IT For decades, women have been sold a particular vision of liberation. Prioritize your career. Maximize your independence. Explore your sexuality without consequence. Reject marriage, delay motherhood, and never compromise your ambitions for someone else's needs. Above all, put yourself first. We were assured that freedom from traditional obligations would produce unprecedented happiness. TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND If that were true, we would certainly see it in society. But instead, what was promised as empowerment has delivered emptiness. Despite constant technological connectivity, loneliness and social isolation remain pervasive. Anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation are serious concerns, particularly among younger generations. These problems have many causes, and attributing them all to feminism would be intellectually dishonest. But ignoring the possibility that our prevailing philosophy has failed to deliver its promised fulfillment would be equally foolish. We’ve spent decades dismantling the institutions that tether individuals to one another, only to discover that autonomy is a poor substitute for belonging. Perhaps most tragically, we’ve taught women to regard sacrifice as oppression rather than an indispensable part of love. Consider the contradiction. A woman who sacrifices her time, energy, and health to climb the corporate ladder is celebrated as ambitious. A woman making comparable sacrifices for her husband and children is too often regarded as having surrendered her potential to the patriarchy. Why? ONE GROUP OF MARRIED AMERICANS IS HAVING MORE SEX — AND HAPPIER MARRIAGES I am profoundly grateful for the opportunities women have today. I’ve competed as a collegiate athlete, traveled the country, built a career, and achieved things my younger self could never have imagined. But no professional accolade, public recognition, or personal achievement has given me the satisfaction and purpose I’ve found in marriage and motherhood. They require more of me than anything I've ever done (even a 200-yard butterfly). It's hard. But "hard" and "bad" are not synonymous. Motherhood fundamentally changed my understanding of success. There's something remarkably clarifying about being needed by someone who has nothing to offer you in return except themselves. I don't view it as a limitation on my freedom, but instead a revelation of what my freedom is for. Which brings me back to Cooper, who just welcomed her first child with her husband. I genuinely congratulate her. But there's irony in continuing to promote perpetual self-prioritization through meaningless hookups and "girl-bossing" while building a life rooted in the very institutions modern feminism so often characterizes as oppressive. Perhaps motherhood will offer her the same perspective it offered me: that the deepest fulfillment isn't found in putting yourself first, but in loving someone enough to put them first. Of course, marriage and motherhood aren't the only paths to meaning. Women who are single, childless, or unable to have children are no less valuable. Purpose takes countless forms, but lasting meaning generally requires looking beyond ourselves. This is hardly a novel insight. Christianity has taught for centuries that a life centered exclusively on the self is ultimately impoverished. Love is not merely a feeling to be pursued while convenient. It is a commitment expressed through action, fidelity, humility, and sacrifice. Our culture treats these virtues as antiquated burdens, then wonders why so many feel unmoored. Cooper and Bush's advice is troubling because it reduces marriage to personal optimization. Marriage becomes less a covenant to honor than an arrangement to continually reassess against hypothetical alternatives. There are legitimate reasons marriages end, including abuse and betrayal. But reflexively encouraging people to search for something better without acknowledging the responsibilities of commitment isn't teaching empowerment like the self-proclaimed feminists like to claim. It teaches disposability. A generation encouraged to keep every option open may eventually discover that life's most meaningful commitments require closing certain doors. Choosing a spouse. Raising children. Building a family. Practicing faith. Serving a community. Creating something that will endure long after your own ambitions have faded. Like everything associated with risk, these commitments impose limits, but I’ve found they also give life its depth. Women deserve more than the hollow assurance that happiness is perpetually waiting in the next relationship, promotion, or reinvention of themselves. They deserve to know that fulfillment isn't always found in acquiring more and finding someone that validates your every desire. Often, it's found in giving more. The great lie of modern empowerment isn't that women are capable of extraordinary things. It's that a life devoted primarily to ourselves is the most extraordinary thing we can aspire to. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We should stop telling women that the ultimate goal is to have everything and start reminding them of the beauty of having something worth giving everything for. And perhaps the grass isn't always greener on the other side. It’s greener where you water it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM RILEY GAINES
news.summary: Alex Cooper and Sophia Bush's viral marriage advice sparks a deeper debate about feminism, sacrifice, and what empowerment truly means for women.

news.title: Elon Musk threatens to go after Democrats' puppeteers after hearing their post-election plan to attack him
news.text:
Tech trillionaire Elon Musk issued a warning to Democrats after hearing their plans to investigate him over his time in the Trump administration.

Musk was responding to an article with a bevy of comments from Democrats saying they will hound him and his many companies if they win power in the midterm elections.

'Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.' 

Democrats have long accused Musk of having various conflicts of interest with the actions he took when he headed up the Department of Government Efficiency.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword. Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets …" he wrote Wednesday on X, the social media platform he owns.

In another post, he responded to liberal talking head Kara Swisher claiming Musk could have been in jail if Kamala Harris had won the 2024 presidential election.

"And that's not because she's some avenging fury. It's because there's a lot of questions around different companies of his," she said.

"If Donald Trump loses the House and the Senate ... I'd be worried if I were him! No matter how rich he is, there are all these agencies, some of which he put a knife in and killed in the DOGE, many of whom were investigating him," she claimed. "He stopped half a dozen investigations of his various companies."

Musk responded simply, "Message received."

Democrat Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington pointed to recent allegations that Musk had restricted Ukraine's use of Starlink internet ahead of a damaging Russian attack.

"What happens when one guy gets a giant contract from the government and then uses it to do something that shuts down communication in a war that has been extremely important to the United States to support Ukraine?” she said.

"Congress must demand a full accounting of the damage Mr. Musk and DOGE caused, and we will not let anyone obstruct our oversight," said Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), who is also a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. 

Spokespeople for Musk did not respond to multiple requests from Politico for comment.

news.title: Trumpworld Insider Reveals His Embarrassing ‘Jesus’ Error
news.text:
View host Alyssa Farah Griffin, an aide in the first Trump administration, said her former boss had an embarrassing theory about Jesus Christ’s real name.

Griffin, 37, revealed the humiliating flub in a post on X. Replying to a user who wondered what the “H” in Jesus H. Christ stood for, Griffin shared, “Hand on my heart, my first day at the White House, Trump asked me if I knew what the ‘H’ stood for. I said no. He said, Horatio.” She added, “I think about that at least once a week. 😭” 

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the most widely accepted historical theory for Jesus’ middle initial is that in the early Christian church, the first three letters of Jesus’ name in Greek were written as ΙΗΣ or IHS—which sparked confusion in Latin-speaking translations that frequently misread the “divine monogram” as the Latin letter H. 

Folklore suggests the “H” became a stand-in for “Harold,” over time, after people regularly misheard the “Hallowed be thy name” part of “The Lord’s Prayer.”

Griffin, a Republican former media strategist who also worked for Mike Pence and Mark Meadows and served as Pentagon press secretary, became The View’s resident conservative co-host in 2022, when she filled the spot left by Meghan McCain when she departed the year before. Griffin’s X post follows her 2024 announcement on The View that she’d voted for a Democrat for the first time when she cast her vote for Kamala Harris. 

She resigned from Trump’s administration after breaking with him over his repeated denials that he lost the 2020 election. “I made the decision to step down in December because I saw where this was heading, and I wasn’t comfortable being a part of sharing this message to the public that the election results might go a different way,” she wrote in an op-ed for Politico in 2021. “I didn’t see that to be where the facts lay.”

You see a real decline in him. It’s a fact you can’t get past,” she said at the time. “Our country is so polarized that Trump supporters see that and they don’t think a thing about it. [They say] ‘He’s my tough guy, he’s my fighter,’ but they see any gaffe of Joe Biden’s, and Joe Biden is ‘aging,’ and he’s ‘too old.’ It’s a Rorschach test of where the country is.”

Griffin remains the show’s most frequent defender of conservative causes, in contrast to her fellow host, former Republican strategist and fierce Trump critic Ana Navarro, who, though still a registered Republican, campaigned for Harris in 2024.

Griffin’s anecdote aligns with her frequent critiques of the president’s performance since regaining office. “‘Why are elections only stolen when he loses?’ is my question,” Griffin said as Trump geared up to address the nation again in July to deny the 2020 election. “My thing is, Mr. President, focus on the election you won. You won in 2024. You won every battleground state. You won the popular vote.” 

“You need to focus on that because voters voted for you, thinking you were going to address the cost of living. You were going to deal with the border,” she concluded.
