news.title: Midterm Shocker: The Polls Are Full of Crap — and Black Voters Just Might Save America
news.text:
When you’re a two-ply man on a one-ply budget, life gets messy. You empathize with Lady Macbeth’s hands.

Sure, you’re extra-careful. Maybe even methodical. (Everyone has their own technique.) But, alas, most of the time you still get [expletive] results.

Which is a perfect analogy for modern-day polling, because that entire industry is one-ply, too. Pollsters lack the budget to poll tens of thousands of people in million-plus communities, so they use guesswork, statistical projections, and sweeping assumptions about strangers.

Thirty years ago, when the internet was a novelty and everyone answered their landlines, cold calls had a very high success rate. Voters were willing (and often excited) to talk. A decade later, it took three calls to reach one respondent.

And today? 

Check out this 2024 article from the Washington Post:

[N]obody answers their phone anymore.Pew Research Center’s Courtney Kennedy is one of the nation’s most-cited polling methods experts. When she started in this business two decades ago, you had to call about three random numbers to get one to answer, a low response rate that already was sending tremors through the polling industry.By last year, Pew had to hit up about 140 random numbers to get that one response. [emphasis added]

Garbage in, garbage out. When only one out of 140 people is willing to participate, there’s just no way it’ll produce reliable results. 

Because you’ve filtered out the normies.

And instead, your data is top-heavy with lonely weirdos with nothing better to do than respond to political polls — often because they’re WAY more ideologically driven than the Average Joe. It’s probably why so many polls greatly exaggerated the strength of DSA candidates, projecting that Abdul El-Sayed would win the Democratic primary by 10 points (he won in a one-point squeaker) and Francesca Hong would win by 22 (she lost by half a point).

Assuming, of course, that the polls are real. Which isn’t always true.

But the weirdest, strangest, most utterly inexplicable question of the 2026 midterm polling is this: Why are the Democrats overperforming in red states — and BADLY underperforming in blue states?

This is supposed to be a blue wave election. Donald Trump is supposed to be the most unpopular president since Harry Truman. There have been countless news stories about the Democrats pulling jaw-dropping upsets in ruby-red states like Texas, Mississippi, Iowa, South Carolina, Montana, Kansas, and more.

Yet in blue states like Michigan, Minnesota, Maine, and New Hampshire, the Republican Senate candidates are all within striking distance — which is more consistent with a RED WAVE election!

Possible explanations: Candidate quality (or lack thereof) is the real story. Maybe the Democrats are overperforming in South Carolina because the Republican Senate candidate is unusually weak — and maybe the Republicans are overperforming in Michigan for a similar reason.

I’m sure it’s a factor. Quality matters. 

When voters can choose between sane and Cypress Hill, they usually side with sane.

And it’s also true that each state is unique. Maine voters are more concerned about the Canadian border; Texans care more about Mexico’s. Somali fraud is a huge issue in Minnesota; less so in Kansas. What plays in Peoria might bomb in Biloxi.

Perhaps drawing national conclusions from state-specific elections is a fool’s errand. 

But I doubt it. Because millions of Americans will be voting in every state. (More than 14 million already have.) The two national political parties are battling for control of Capitol Hill — and the contrast between the two has never been more glaring.

To paraphrase Barry Goldwater, this isn’t an “echo” election. It’s a “choice” election.

And it’s a helluva choice: MAGA versus the DSA. The battle lines are crystal clear.

Furthermore, the biggest issues of the 2026 midterms are all national issues: affordability, inflation, gas prices, AI/data centers, immigration, the Iran War, Israel/Gaza, trans, and (of course) President Trump. Because the sitting president is ALWAYS on the ballot in midterm elections.

If this isn’t a national election, I don’t know what is!

We all know about the historic headwinds: The party in power almost always takes it on the chin. That should be twice as true for a president with the lowest approval ratings since Harry Truman.

So if these numbers are right, the Democrats ought to be dominating.

Yet that’s simply not happening in blue states. DSA-aligned candidates are struggling. There’s a very real risk the Dems will LOSE Senate seats in Michigan, Minnesota, and New Hampshire! And even though Kamala Harris won Maine by seven points, Republican incumbent Susan Collins is still within the margin of error against her left-wing opponent.

Something is undermining their coalition. 

It’s a group that was once loyal, but is now wandering in the wilderness. A group that’s bleeding Democratic support — because the party is no longer their home.

Which is making mincemeat of polling predictions and predictive models: These voters aren’t behaving like WE think they’re supposed to!

I’m talking about black voters.

Sixteen years ago, black people voted 95% Democrat. By 2020, 77% of black adults identified as Democrats. And in 2023, the number fell to just 66%.

From Axios:

A generational and structural shift is decoupling Black identity from Democratic Party loyalty, transforming a once-reliable voting bloc into a cohort of "political free agents" that the GOP is uniquely positioned to exploit.[…]By the numbers: Republican identification among Black Americans climbed into the mid-to-high teens in recent Gallup data.Trump surged to an average near 20% approval among Black voters in the first quarter of 2025, nearly double his approval at the same point in his first term, according to Gallup.That was driven largely by Black men and those moving toward Republican affiliation.

Also relevant is religious affiliation: 73% of black people are Christian, compared to 62% of white people. Black people are also more likely than white people to attend church and engage in “religious practices.” 

Just 39% of white people called the Bible “very important” — compared to 70% of black people. Black Americans are (roughly) twice as likely to read the Bible daily and pray daily.

Which might be why black voters are rejecting the anti-Christian, pro-Islam positioning of the DSA.

If Abdul El-Sayed had 2008-level black support, he’d win Michigan’s Senate seat in a cakewalk. The Republicans wouldn’t have a chance. This election would already be over.

But in the Michigan primary, black voters rejected El-Sayed, voting en masse for his (white) opponent, Haley Stevens.

From The Hill:

[Haley Stevens] led El-Sayed by 8 percentage points in districts where more than 15 percent of the population is Black. Polling in July showed that just 21 percent of Black voters backed El-Sayed while 67 percent supported the House Democrat.A Michigan Education Survey also showed El-Sayed struggling with Black voters. Stevens notched 69 percent from the bloc; El-Sayed garnered 37 percent support.

Stevens made no secret of her support for Israel. That’s probably one of the reasons why she did so well with black voters.

From Fox News:

[A]ccording to the Fox News poll, African Americans were the racial group most likely to say the U.S. isn't supportive enough of Israel when asked the question along with White and Hispanic voters. That number was 25% compared with 19% for Hispanic voters and 15% for White voters.African American voters were also the least likely of the three groups to agree that America was too supportive of Israel, with 40% disagreeing as compared to White voters at 44% and Hispanic voters at 56%.The stat stands sharply against the ubiquitous notion that African Americans — owing to supposed shared experiences of injustice and oppression — organically align with the Palestinian experience.

Meanwhile, the DSA movement doesn’t exactly mirror the Rainbow Coalition: According to a 2021 survey, 85% of DSA members are white, and 80% have college degrees. It’s whiter than mayonnaise on a polar bear.

As the DSA wrests control of the Democratic Party, black voters are walking away.

This has flipped the dynamics of the 2026 midterms. It’s why the pollsters’ models are garbage: They’re relying on voting projections that no longer apply.

Black voters aren’t gonna vote 90% for El-Sayed. It ain’t happening. Millions will vote for his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. 

Many won’t vote at all.

And until a new voting pattern emerges that can be tracked, predicted, and quantified in polling models, none of these polls mean anything. They don’t have the budget to interview thousands of people, and their base model is simply wrong. We know this because they’ve been wrong consistently and repeatedly.

"This is our modern-day 'Dewey Defeats Truman'" -@ChuckTodd #ElectionNight https://t.co/sdij0Iaa1e— TODAY (@TODAYshow) November 9, 2016

It’s now 2026. Not 2016, 2008, or 1992. If pollsters botched elections when people still answered phones — and when large demos still voted predictably — what do you think will happen when they don’t?

Because, very clearly, black people are voting differently. (And they’re not the only ones.) It’s a brave new world. Polling data hasn’t caught up.

Yet we’re still extrapolating group decisions on any weirdo who’s willing to take a poll that 139 other people have already rejected!

So OF COURSE these polling results are full of [expletive]. It’s one-ply technology in a two-ply world. Flush it away and start over.

And don’t look now, but black voters are the wildcard of the 2026 midterms. If El-Sayed and his DSA-aligned brethren go down in defeat, it’ll be because of black voters. They’re our wall between sanity and Cypress Hill.

God bless ‘em. They just might save America.

One Last Thing: 2026 will reach a crescendo with the midterm elections. Nothing less than the future of our country teeters in the balance.

Never before have the political battle lines been so clearly defined. Blue wave or red wall, the 2026 midterms will transform our country.

news.title: The View co-host shares Trump anecdote she thinks about weekly
news.text:
The View co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin is reflecting on her time working for Donald Trump’s administration during his first term.

In response to a tweet speculating about the origins of the expletive phrase “Jesus H. Christ,” the 37-year-old offered up what the president told her on the subject when she worked as his special assistant.

“Hand on my heart, my first day at the White House, Trump asked me if I knew what the H stood for,” Griffin wrote Thursday on X. “I said no. He said Horatio.”

She added: “I think about that at least once a week.”

The saying is a profane interjection typically used to show anger, surprise or shock. The “H” does not stand for a real middle name, and the expression likely came from Greek letters, although the exact origins are unknown.

Griffin was appointed special assistant to the president and press secretary to former Vice President Mike Pence in September 2017. Two years later, she became the press secretary for the United States Department of Defense and the director of media affairs, which made her the chief spokesperson for the department. 

In April 2020, Griffin joined the White House Office as the White House communications director under Trump, making her the only person to have held all three of those positions. She resigned from the role in December 2020.

After joining CNN as a political contributor in 2021, Griffin was named co-host of The View starting with season 26 in 2022. She currently sits at the table alongside Whoopi Goldberg, Joy Behar, Sara Haines, Ana Navarro and Sunny Hostin.

Griffin is known for sharing her expert political insight and providing commentary that leans conservative.

However, her relationship with Trump seems to have soured in the years since she resigned. She voted for Trump’s opponent Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election — marking her first time voting for a Democrat.

Last year, Trump took aim at Griffin after she broke her promise that she would wear a MAGA hat on the show when the Israeli hostages were released.

The president said that after Griffin resigned, she sent him two glowing letters. However, Trump said he “never thought [she] was very outstanding. I figured she would not make it. And she didn’t have a big role here, either.”

He went on to blame the ABC daytime talk show for Griffin’s changed stance on him, saying: “And then, she got hired by The View, and they gave her a couple of bucks, and she changed her view very quickly.”

“I never thought she’d make it,” he said again. “Never thought she had what it took.”

news.title: FCC Chair Brendan Carr Echoes Trump, Threatens Broadcasters Over 'Fake Polls'
news.text:
Once again, a member of President Donald Trump's administration is threatening to punish private citizens for their speech using the power of the government.

Specifically, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) threatened broadcasters who dare to report on polls the president doesn't approve of. Even if the complaint were valid, it would be difficult to enforce without violating the First Amendment.

"During this election season, there has been a significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls designed to do nothing more than interfere with the regular functioning of the electoral process and alter the normal patterns of voter turnout and enthusiasm," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr wrote on X. "Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis."

Carr is directly adopting Trump's terminology, in addition to his erratic capitalization: The president often uses the term suppression polls to describe surveys that don't reflect in his favor. The implication is that these polls are manufactured to conceal or downplay enthusiasm for Trump or his preferred candidates, making it less likely that his supporters will turn out if they think it's a lost cause.

Carr doesn't single out any offenders, though there are some likely examples. This week, purported pollster Wedgewood Polls revealed that as part of an "experimental project," it had released surveys with "fabricated numbers" that were printed by outlets like FiftyPlusOne (which sussed out the fraud) and The New York Times.

Similarly, in August, Median Strategies withdrew two polls, then revealed that it had fabricated the results for a "social experiment."

Each scenario is deplorable. And depending on what promises were made, it's possible one firm or the other could face legal consequences.

But it's hard to see how a news outlet could face legal reprisal for just reporting the results of a survey it thought was conducted accurately.

"The FCC takes these issues seriously," Carr added. "Broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes. It is important that broadcasters comply with their public interest obligations."

There are indeed rules against news distortion and broadcast hoaxes, but they're narrowly tailored to avoid conflicting with the First Amendment.

"News distortion 'must involve a significant event and not merely a minor or incidental aspect of the news report,'" according to the FCC. In addition, "broadcasters are only subject to enforcement if it can be proven that they have deliberately distorted a factual news report. Expressions of opinion or errors stemming from mistakes are not actionable."

The hoax rule, on the other hand, is even less applicable: It involves "broadcasting false information concerning a crime or a catastrophe," where the broadcaster "knows this information is false" and can foreseeably "cause substantial public harm" but airs it anyway, and the broadcast then "does in fact directly cause substantial public harm."

In other words, neither standard applies to a broadcaster that covered an inaccurate poll, especially without knowing at the time that it was wrong.

"Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong," Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic FCC commissioner, wrote on X. "FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith."

Carr doesn't specify what he thinks should happen to any offenders, though since he tends to define "public interest" as whatever Trump says, we can make an educated guess.

Right before the 2024 presidential election, The Des Moines Register published a poll that found then–Vice President Kamala Harris leading Trump in Iowa by three percentage points. Trump ended up winning the state by 13 percentage points, but he was apparently so upset by the poll that he sued both the Register and pollster Ann Selzer, claiming the inaccurate survey constituted "brazen election interference" that violated the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act.

It was clear at the time that the lawsuit was completely meritless. Just as Carr suggested this week in his social media post, Trump was trying to create an exception to the First Amendment for "fake news."

"In the United States there is no such thing as a claim for 'fraudulent news,'" Robert Corn-Revere, chief counsel at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, wrote in a motion on the defendants' behalf. "No court in any jurisdiction has ever held such a cause of action might be valid, and few plaintiffs have ever attempted to bring such outlandish claims."

A judge agreed and dismissed the lawsuit last month.

"If someone is accurately reporting the results of a poll, that wouldn't be a false statement," UCLA law professor Rick Hasen told The Washington Post at the time. "The poll might have errors in it, but that wouldn't be a false statement."

That's as true then as it is now. Unless he can somehow prove that a broadcaster knew a pollster had faked a survey, there's no way Carr can punish someone for reporting on the results without running afoul of the First Amendment.

"Brendan Carr is not the journalism police. And he is just about the least qualified person in the country to lecture the press about journalistic ethics," Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in an emailed statement. "News broadcasters have a First Amendment right to report polling data, even if it proves to be inaccurate, just like they have a First Amendment right to report on Carr and Trump's own countless lies and distortions, even when they turn out to be inaccurate. FCC policies about hoaxes and distortions must be applied narrowly to avoid clashing with the Constitution, if they can be constitutionally applied at all."
news.summary: Once again, Carr is playing defense for his boss in a way that would clearly run afoul of the First Amendment.

news.title: A Sheriff Called Maryland “Disneyland for Illegal Immigrants.” Can a Wedding Photographer Oust Him?
news.text:
Hoping that someone else would step up and throw their hat in the ring, Lana Foley waited until the last day to file her candidacy for the top elected law enforcement job in Wicomico County on the Eastern Shore of Maryland. Foley, a wedding and portrait photographer, has no law enforcement background nor had she ever intended to run for office. Now, she is challenging the incumbent Republican sheriff of 20 years who faced no opposition in the last four elections. “I’ve had people ask me, why didn’t you run for board of education?” Foley said. “Why didn’t you run for county council? Why didn’t you run for county executive? I felt like the sheriff role is one of the most influential roles that you can have in a community.” 

Foley grew up in a Republican household in Indiana but she has called Maryland home for decades. After being denied coverage for treatment of a thyroid cancer in 2013, Foley said she switched her allegiance to the Democratic Party because of Obamacare. She supported Kamala Harris in 2024 and, when Donald Trump was re-elected, she started Crabs on the Shore, a local branch of the national women-led mobilization group Red, Wine & Blue.

The chapter began as a support system. “We do have a pretty big red area down here,” she said, “and I just didn’t want people to feel alone in their fear or concerns.” Then, last year, Foley and others started speaking up against a proposed collaboration between the county and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Her opponent Sheriff Mike Lewis—running for his sixth consecutive term—was an enthusiastic proponent of a 287(g) agreement that would allow local officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on immigrants in jail to transfer them to ICE custody, and he sought to bring it to their community. 

“He’s a firm believer in wanting immigrants out of our country,” Foley said, even though this might not be a popular position in Wicomico County, which has the largest share of Haitian residents of any county in the state. She added that one possible explanation for his long tenure could be as simple as having no other “option to even question his success as a sheriff.”

Encouraged by friends and family, in February, Foley decided to make the leap and launch her campaign. This November, she’s looking to offer an alternative on the ballot and, against the odds, defeat a popular law-and-order sheriff in a Republican-leaning rural county. Working in her favor is the growing rejection of the Trump administration’s draconian anti-immigration policies that have spread fear across US communities.

“While Trump rode the wave of discontent back into office in 2024,” said Niambi Carter, a University of Maryland associate professor who researches public opinion and political behavior around immigration, “his cruelty turned the tide on that same anti-immigration sentiment.” 

The potential backlash in Wicomico County and in many jurisdictions across the country is a reflection of President Trump “misreading” the extent to which his supporters would stand by his efforts to deport the undocumented population, Carter explained. Conservative voters, she said, view immigrants as a “manifestation of the discomfort they feel financially and culturally.” And while they “were fine with the mass deportations of ‘bad’ immigrants—the ‘worst of the worst’—they did not want to see their neighbors and co-workers being rounded up and their lives upended.” What has led to “Trump’s undoing on this issue,” she noted, has been his administration’s indiscriminate enforcement.”

Largely blue Maryland has seen a ramp up in immigration enforcement since Trump returned to the White House. Between January 2025 and March 2026, ICE made 6,596 arrests in the state—a 257 percent increase compared to the same period the year before, according to the Maryland Immigrant Rights Protection Task Force. In the last couple of months, the agency has continued to conduct enforcement operations throughout the state, often arresting people without a warrant.

This September, a 40-hour blitz in one neighborhood of Frederick turned violent, with reports and videos showing ICE agents beating protesters with batons. The clash prompted Maryland’s Democratic congressional delegation to request an investigation into the agency’s tactics, noting that the vast majority of people caught in the surge of ICE arrests lacked a criminal record.

In Wicomico County, the immigration sweeps have had a chilling effect. The county seat, Salisbury, is home to more than 3,000 Haitians—or roughly 10 percent of the city’s population—many of whom are employed in farms and poultry processing plants, the region’s main economic engine. After the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, making that community more vulnerable to ICE enforcement, flyers advising poultry workers not to leave the house circulated and church attendance noticeably dropped. 

When Sheriff Mike Lewis publicly signaled his interest in entering a formal partnership with ICE last year, he said it would allow his office to “better protect our citizens while upholding the rule of law.” A long-time law-enforcement officer who grew up in the city, he gained national prominence as a “drug warrior” state trooper conducting seizures of cocaine, heroin, and contraband. Lewis has been a vocal Trump supporter and once described Maryland as “a Disneyland for illegal immigrants.” In 2025, the right-wing think tank Claremont Institute named Lewis sheriff of the year. Fellow Sheriff Jeff Gahler of Harford County lauded him as “one of America’s top conservative voices for our sheriffs.”

The proposed Wicomico County 287(g) agreement championed by Lewis would be the first of its kind on the Eastern Shore. These voluntary cooperation deals between local jurisdictions and ICE have multiplied in Maryland in Trump’s second term, jumping from three to nine in less than a year, according to Sebastian Brown, an advocacy strategist on the ACLU of Maryland’s public policy team. Brown lives in Frederick County, whose immigration hardliner sheriff was one of the first in the country to adopt a 287(g) agreement. (He’s also up for re-election this November.)

“The state of fear that folks have been in across the state and the country under the second Trump administration has been the reality here since 2008,” Brown said. “The fear that any interaction with police, including a simple traffic stop, could be a deportation trap.” 

That pioneering controversial agreement has faced resistance—and legal challenges—for a long time. In 2020, Frederick County settled a lawsuit brought by a woman from El Salvador who challenged her arrest by local law enforcement and subsequent transfer to ICE as unlawful and motivated by racial profiling. The following year, the sheriff’s office reached a $125,000 settlement with a Latina immigrant who claimed her detention under 287(g) over a supposed “broken” tail light fit a pattern of “racially discriminatory and unlawful policing.”

“For a while, it was seen as just a problem of Frederick and it wasn’t widely felt,” Brown said. But, he added, as these agreements started cropping up in more than a third of Maryland’s counties, “the opposition spread even to these more broadly conservative counties.”

In Wicomico County, which Trump won by more than 5 percentage points in 2024 and barely carried four years earlier, Lewis’ plans to partner with ICE might have seemed uncontroversial. Wicomico has a Republican-majority council and GOP county executive. “They thought it would just be a slam dunk,” Brown said.

It wasn’t. When news came out in the summer of 2025 that the sheriff’s office had contacted ICE about an agreement, the reaction was fierce. “It just felt like a slap in the face to our community members,” Foley said, “and so we basically jumped in headfirst as quickly as we could.”

The ACLU of Maryland urged the county not to buy into a “program designed to scapegoat immigrants for political gain.” By the fall, the civil rights organization had joined forces with groups such as CATA, a farmworkers support committee, and Foley’s Crabs on the Shore, to protest the proposed deal. “The 287(g) program isn’t about safety,” Foley said at a rally in Salisbury that September. “It’s about fear and control.”

Foley was one of dozens of community members, advocates, and business owners who spoke up against it in council meetings in Salisbury. During a five-hour, standing-room only public comment session in October 2025, one Haitian-born man who has lived in Wicomico County for more than 40 years said he had previously voted for Lewis, but disagreed with him on the issue of local cooperation with ICE. Another speaker told the council how a member of her Haitian church had her husband taken away by ICE one month after their baby was born. “287(g) is a devastation to the Haitian community,” a Haitian resident said, while calling Lewis a “sensible” man. “We built this community.” 

“A lot of people who supported even the current administration,” said Monica Brooks, president of the Wicomico County chapter of the NAACP, “they don’t support 287(g) and what’s happening with immigration.” The issue “brought a whole bunch of folks to the other side,” she added, including farmers. “There are people who were still all in until they saw families taken and separated right in our backyard.”

Facing increasing pushback, Wicomico County put plans to enter an agreement on hold, only to announce in January that it would be moving forward with it. But then, in February, Maryland Governor Wes Moore signed into law a statewide ban on 287(g) agreements, forcing counties to drop their deals with ICE. Lewis went to Annapolis to testify against the new law, which he has criticized for putting “partisan politics over public safety.” 

Grudgingly Wicomico County complied and County Executive Julie Giordano informed ICE that they were only withdrawing from the program because of the legislation. “It is the biggest betrayal to law enforcement and public safety that I have ever seen,” Lewis said of the abolition of 287(g) programs, warning that, in the absence of this cooperation, ICE would have no choice but to swoop into the community. “There is a huge disconnect between him and people of color in the community,” Brooks said. “And I’ve not seen him try to do anything to fix that.” Lewis didn’t respond to an email request for an interview.

Jenkis and Lewis are among a group of 17 sheriffs who have since filed a lawsuit to block the enforcement of another law, the Community Trust Act, which places limits on how state and local law enforcement can assist ICE with requests to hold someone and transfer them to the agency’s custody. In opposing this law, they claim they “will be required to violate their oaths of office.” The sheriffs were represented by the Federation for American Immigration Reform, a Washington, DC-based organization that wants to restrict immigration and was labeled a “hate group” by the Southern Poverty Law Center. (The Trump administration has also sued the state of Maryland over the legislation.)

In June, Lewis won the Republican primary with 5,126 votes—or 76 percent—defeating his first challenger in a long time: Scott Hamilton, a retired military aviator. “I have faced zero opposition since the day I was elected,” Lewis said at a fundraiser for the Harford County sheriff’s re-election. “Zero opposition. But this year I have an opponent. I have a former deputy who is running against me for the first time in 20 years. His slogan is ‘less politics, more service.’ I felt like saying, ‘Bitch, you have no idea what it’s like to be a sheriff. It’s all about politics.'”

During a recent candidate forum, Lewis said he was frustrated with the Community Trust Act because it stopped his office from doing a “smooth, secure transaction” with ICE. But in a show of moderation, he added, “I’ve reflected on a number of things I’ve said over the years and it primarily has to do with immigration,” and then he promised “greater self-awareness.”

Meanwhile, Foley has tried to present her lack of law enforcement credentials not as a drawback, but as an advantage; an opportunity to bring a fresh perspective to the office. She garnered 4,710 votes in the Democratic primary. In the last push before the general election, Foley held a meet-and-greet event in October and was planning on being at the polls every day during early voting week.

Lewis’ campaign has far outdone Foley’s fundraising, bringing in more than $32,000 in contributions against her $3,363. “He’s used to having a certain degree of popularity with some folks,” Brooks said of Lewis. “But you have a newcomer who’s never run for office, who’s not even law enforcement, who did really well in the primary, and that tells me that people want something new.”

Foley hopes that a push for change after 20 years, a general rejection of Trump’s immigration enforcement overreach, and her message of restoring trust in the community will prevail. She acknowledged that she was unsure if her relative success was primarily propelled by the community’s support for immigration. “But I’m sure it’s not hurting for people to know that I’ve been fighting for our immigrant community,” Foley said, “and that I’m going to continue to do that.”

news.title: Voting For Keisha Lance Bottoms Is More Important Than Liking Her
news.text:
Choosing a candidate who truly represents you is an ideal often reserved for white men in American politics. And since politics are often an exercise in practicality over preference, Georgia voters need to be pragmatic on Election Day.

Keisha Lance Bottoms is the best choice for governor.

Liking her isn’t a requirement; preventing her opponent from being elected is.

Former President Barack Obama is set to join Bottoms and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff for a rally in Atlanta during the final week of October, as the campaign has called in the big dogs to give her one final boost before the election. Like so many Black women before her who have tried to reach the highest seats in American politics, the conversation is less about Bottoms’ accomplishments and more about picking apart who she is, or isn’t.

“Most Democrats who are being honest are nervous about the campaign of Mayor Bottoms, who, to be clear, brings a lot of strengths to the race,” Andrew Heaton, a Georgia-based Democratic strategist, told Politico during the spring. “[Republicans] are going to have to find messages against the other candidates. They’ve already got the attack ads on Mayor Bottoms written.”

Critics often highlight superficial issues, whether it was her decision not to seek a second term as mayor of Atlanta, the way she went about handling a global pandemic — in which Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican, attempted to sue her for enforcing a mask mandate when millions were dying during the peak of COVID-19 — or the fact that a Black woman from Atlanta can’t properly cook macaroni and cheese. This type of “hate” is something Black women too often experience — just ask Stacey Abrams and Kamala Harris.

According to MSNOW, fifty-seven percent of eligible Black voters live in the South, as Georgia serves as the state with the third-largest Black population, with the Atlanta metropolitan area hosting the second-most Black residents in the country. Given the history of the state of Georgia and Atlanta serving as the home of civil rights movements and Black economic and cultural empowerment for decades, as well as being the face of overt voter suppression and racism, the idea of having an HBCU alum (Florida A&M) who is a former judge, city council member, mayor, and senior White House adviser on the precipice of making history, despite the current administration, seems like the perfect time for voters and Democrats of all colors — but specifically Black ones — to fall in line instead of hemming and hawing over inconsequential pet peeves.

Look around, this isn’t the time to sit out elections because a perfect candidate isn’t on the ballot.

Since 2005, Georgia has had a Republican trifecta, giving the GOP control of the Governor’s mansion, the state senate, and the state house of representatives for over two decades. With a Bottoms win or a legislative victory, Democrats in Georgia could finally regain some power. To put things in proper context, Republicans have been in control of one of the Blackest states in America — four years before the Swag Surfin’ was invented.

“I’m going to make sure that Georgia’s the best place to do business and reduce affordability to the lowest it’s ever been, and I’m going to be this man’s favorite governor,” Bottoms’ opponent, Rick Jackson, said at a campaign rally this summer as he pointed at Donald Trump. Just like the occupant of the Oval Office, Jackson is a billionaire, political newcomer, and businessman who thinks the answer to every issue is a mathematical one, despite siding with a man who has proven that he only cares about figures that go into his bank account. “Affordability is not a political problem. Affordability is a business problem,” declared Jackson. “It requires business solutions, just like this man’s [Trump] been doing all his life.”

In a year when midterm election results could shift the future of this country, the South has been at the center of that conversation. In Florida, Angie Nixon is trying to do the impossible: win a statewide election without a war chest or national name recognition as a Black female progressive Democrat running for the U.S. Senate. 

And in Georgia, Bottoms is trying to add “Georgia governor” next to “former Atlanta mayor” on her resume. Despite all that, too many are still ignoring their efforts. In August, the Democratic National Committee failed to select Atlanta as the host city for the 2028 Democratic National Convention, announcing Boston, Denver, and Philadelphia as finalists.

“For the DNC to not even include Atlanta in the shortlist means that the DNC does not consider Atlanta or Georgia relevant to the past, present, or future of the Democratic Party. It seems that Ken Martin [Party Chair] doesn’t even believe himself when he said that the road to the White House runs through the South,” Atlanta mayor Andre Dickens wrote in retort to the decision. According to the Associated Press, the party didn’t specify why Georgia’s capital city wasn’t selected. “They are afraid to leave their comfort zone and blind to the fact that the South is the answer,” Dickens declared. “They are abandoning Atlanta, abandoning the South, and once again abandoning Black voters.”

However, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock thinks the Trump administration and the GOP’s consistent, unforgivable mistakes could lead more voters to invest in the South’s untapped political potential, and in candidates like Bottoms.

“What is different about this moment is that we have an administration that is wearing their bigotry on their sleeve,” he said. “The cruelty that we’re seeing unleashed, not only against Black people, but against people of color, against people who are perceived to be other — the cruelty is baked into the cake. It’s their electoral strategy.”

A few weeks ago, Bottoms and Jackson met for what is scheduled to be their only debate. As she took the stage, it reminded everyone that Georgia voters don’t need to be part of “The Keisha Lance Bottoms Fan Club.” They simply need to recognize that another white man who seeks to operate like Trump isn’t the solution.

“Georgia is a work in progress, and we’ve got a lot of work to do, but we have the power to make Georgia more affordable, to protect a woman’s right to choose, to protect our voting rights, to protect our communities from out-of-control data center growth, to make sure every child has the opportunity to reach their God-given potential, and to make sure we are protected from the harmful policies of Donald Trump,” Bottoms explained. “What we do in this moment will echo through history, so let’s choose hope over fear, progress over division, and come together to build a better Georgia for everyone. While my opponent is running to enrich himself and be Trump’s favorite governor, I want to be yours, Georgia, and I hope to earn your vote.”

America is a mess right now because millions of people couldn’t stomach the idea of voting for an overqualified Black woman. Let’s hope that the citizens of Georgia have learned from the mistakes of this country. 

Electing Keisha Lance Bottoms won’t compensate for Kamala Harris’ loss, but it would give us a reason to believe that America isn’t as dumb as it seems.

Georgia: vote with your head, not your misogynoir.

news.summary: For the second time in the last decade, Bottoms is serving as the last line of defense in one of Black America’s hubs.

news.title: Kamala Just Revealed That She's Running for President in 2028
news.text:
Kamala Harris insists she hasn't decided whether she's running for president in 2028, but she accidentally gave the game away.

Obviously, nobody in the Democrat Party is exactly begging her to jump in. The establishment has been pushing back hard on the idea of a third Kamala campaign. Former allies and donors grumble that she squandered her first year out of office, and they can't come up with a single reason voters should take another look at her. Even her husband, Doug Emhoff, reportedly isn't thrilled about her running again.

You'd think all that would give her pause. Instead, Kamala keeps dropping hints, and her latest one came at an event in Las Vegas, where she debuted a slower, lower-pitched speaking style. It's the newest entry in her long record of changing her voice and speech cadence depending on who's sitting in the audience.

"That era of feeling powerless — like what can we do, this just keeps happening — that era is over because we are now 13 days away from doing something about it to stop the pain," Kamala said, speaking slowly and in a lower register, as if to a room of sleepy kindergarteners.

She kept up the same condescending tone while urging Nevada voters to back Democrats in the state's governor's race and for Congress.

"So that's where we are right now, and that's kind of exciting," she continued. "Right? This is some good stuff. Like, we're taking our power, we're using it, to determine who will hold offices like being the governor of Nevada. Which is so important for the people everyday on the most basic issues that affect our lives. Who will continue to walk those halls of Congress, being an extraordinary fighter."

Kamala Harris just spoke in Las Vegas and it seems she's testing out a new oratory style. It's worse than you can imagine. https://t.co/wzglFWAUBJ— End Wokeness (@EndWokeness) October 21, 2026

This new tone she’s adopting fits how Democrats see voters: as children they need to control. You don't talk to grown adults that way unless you think they need a nap and a juice box before they can handle a ballot.

Let’s be fair: Kamala didn't invent the fake accent. Hillary Clinton infamously slipped into a Southern drawl while campaigning in the South during the 2008 presidential primaries. Barack Obama was known for adjusting his dialect for different crowds during that same campaign. And Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) has been pulling the same trick for years.

It's phony and desperate, every single time.

ICYMI: Ilhan Omar’s Answer on Marrying Her Brother Was Just Painfully Bad

The motive here isn't complicated. Politicians who put on fake accents want voters to feel they share something with them. When a Democrat suddenly picks up a Southern drawl, leans into black vernacular, or shifts her cadence to match the crowd, it's not random or subconscious; it’s a calculated move. The candidate is trying to manufacture cultural familiarity, hoping voters will see her as one of their own. It’s just shameless pandering from a candidate who wants to convey “I’m just like you” without saying the words.

And Kamala wouldn't bother with any of this if she weren't planning to run for president.

Nobody road-tests a new voice for a midterm rally out of civic duty. You do it because you're auditioning for something bigger. So she can keep saying she hasn't made up her mind. Kamala just told us she's running for president.

news.title: Will Elon Musk Be the October Surprise?
news.text:
A version of the below article first appeared in David Corn’s newsletter, Our Land. The newsletter comes out twice a week (most of the time) and provides behind-the-scenes stories and articles about politics, media, and culture. Subscribing costs just $5 a month—but you can sign up for a free 30-day trial.

As I’ve noted in previous issues, I’m now co-hosting a pop-up video podcast on the midterms called Stress Test with award-winning video producer Garrison Hayes. (You can catch the latest episode here.) The name refers to the challenge American democracy is currently facing. With an authoritarian demagogue in the White House, can the United States conduct free and fair elections that produce results that will be widely respected? Can the US political system reject the Donald Trump virus that undermines the rule of law and threatens the constitutional republic? Will it survive the stress placed upon it by a president who tried to overturn a previous election and who has already begun to subvert this one with false accusations of fraud?

In each episode, Garrison and I ask our guests what’s stressing them out about the midterms. My answer, as of today, is the possibility of a last-minute intervention of big money and disinformation, yielding an October surprise that influences one or more of the House and Senate races determining which party ends up controlling Congress. And standing at the intersection of obscenely huge campaign donations and potentially harmful false narratives is a jerk named Elon Musk.

Last week, there was much coverage of the news that Musk has injected $366 million into the midterm elections to aid Trump and the Republicans. (It appears likely his total tab will exceed half a billion dollars.) Much of this money has gone to bolster GOP Senate candidates, particularly the corruption-scarred Ken Paxton in Texas. As pundits and political chatterers pondered the impact of Musk’s millions, my colleague Anna Merlan wisely observed that Musk posed another threat and tagged him the “biggest election disinformation risk.”

She characterized Musk this way after he played a crucial role in spreading the false claim—cooked up by MAGA influencers—that James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, had been absent from the campaign trail because he had checked himself into a mental health hospital in Ohio. The story was 100 percent bullshit. Talarico, according to his campaign, had contracted a nasty bout of the flu, and, after nine or so days out of sight, he was back in public view at the time these MAGA doofuses were asserting he had been in the Ohio facility (which eventually denied Talarico had ever been treated there). Yet the phony tale caught fire and zipped across the internet, largely due to its amplification on the Musk-owned X.

Here’s a fascinating visual depiction of how this crap flew across X:

Musk, as Merlan points out, was a key amplifier of this fraud. He tweeted to his 241.5 million followers—an audience about 100 times the size of Fox News—that the “Talarico campaign is hiding something big that voters ought to know about.” In another post, he maintained, “The Talarico campaign is not being honest about what’s happening.” When the story fell apart, he did not acknowledge he had been wrong. Nor did the MAGA influencers and other right-wingers who had peddled this phony story.

This idiotic assault on Talarico is not likely to lessen his chances of becoming the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in 32 years. But it illustrates a standard play: Start an unfounded and scurrilous rumor about a candidate and use Musk’s platform—perhaps Musk himself—to spread it quickly. If done closer to Election Day, there might not be sufficient time for a candidate to beat back the false accusation. And super-PACs with plenty of cash—from Musk or others (including other Big Tech plutocrats in the AI and crypto fields who are pouring gobs of money into this election)—can do the same: Drop negative ads boosting false allegations in the final week of the campaign. It’s even possible these days for billionaires to use corporate cutouts to finance attack ads anonymously.

With so much at stake—Musk himself has billions of dollars in government contracts he wants to protect or land—it would be surprising if the final days of this campaign were free of disinformation skullduggery and campaign-cash chicanery. (The Russians, too, have started meddling in this election to help the GOP. See the next item.)

The South Africa–born Musk holds an unprecedented position in American politics. With his donations this year, he has made the largest known personal financial contribution to an election, and he controls a social media platform through which political news and disinformation flow, reaching millions of voters—and he himself generates some of that disinformation.

Naturally, Musk warrants continuous scrutiny—especially since he’s a dishonest fellow who’s been promoting the most ludicrous allegations and conspiracy theories for years. During the 2024 campaign, he repeatedly posted the false claim that large numbers of noncitizens were voting, even going so far as to declare that Democrats were flying asylum seekers into swing states and fast-tracking them for citizenship so they could vote. His false or misleading allegations about that election racked up 1.2 billion views on X. He received 134 million views when he reposted an AI-manipulated deepfake video of Kamala Harris supposedly making offensive remarks.

Musk’s conspiracism has extended far beyond election disinformation. He claimed that DEI was the cause of errors in the Los Angeles Fire Department’s response to wildfires and that “white genocide” was underway in South Africa. (Neither allegation was true.) He amplified the fake story that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating pets. He’s resorted to antisemitic tropes to attack George Soros. He falsely charged that millions of dead people were collecting Social Security. (This genius misread the data.) He boosted Russian disinformation that claimed USAID was paying Hollywood celebrities millions of dollars to visit Ukraine, and he put up posts saying USAID funded bioweapons research that included Covid-19. He seconded a meme that proclaimed Pizzagate was “real.” Earlier this year, he amplified a post that said that during the 2020 election, “Pennsylvania sent out 1,823,148 mail-in ballots but received back around 2.5 MILLION mail-in ballots.” This charge—long a mainstay of Trump’s election deniers—has been repeatedly debunked.

That’s a mere sampling. Musk is a nutter. He recently endorsed a social media post that said only men with high testosterone and people with autism should be allowed to engage in governmental “decision making”—sorry, all you gals—and he has shared assorted racist sentiments.

Yet when you’re a trillionaire, your racism, misogyny, antisemitism, ignorance, and conspiracism don’t matter. Republicans have tried to make a scandal of far-left influencer Hasan Piker’s campaigning with Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate, during the primary contest. Yet Musk’s direct aid to a wide range of GOP candidates has not sparked as much of a hullabaloo. Only certain associations seem to be worthy of outrage.

Musk’s influence in the midterms is unparalleled. There’s a lot that could happen in the waning days of this election. Trump, no doubt, is contemplating actions that could cause chaos or spark a crisis. MAGA activists have been urging him to declare martial law—though that would not technically permit him to seize ballots or block elections. Such extreme options aside, an October surprise is more likely to involve disinformation and money. So in the coming weeks, keep your eye on Musk. And in the long run, Americans are going to have to figure out how to keep a schmuck like this from having so much sway in US politics.

news.title: Nolte: Podcaster Jennifer Welch Demands ‘Pistols Firing’ at ‘Antichrist’ JD Vance
news.text:
Jennifer Welch, a left-wing podcaster who has interviewed the biggest names in the Democrat Party, is demanding that there be “pistols firing” at “antichrist” JD Vance to ensure he does not become president in two years.

In a broadcast that is sure to (and should) get the attention of the Secret Service, Welch vomited a pile of hate and violence at our current vice president that only a Democrat could get away with. If a Republican said something like this about Kamala Harris, he or she would be run out of politics.

Keep in mind that Welch is not some fringe podcaster. She is firmly embedded and welcomed in the Democrat Party. Here’s quick list of some of the high-profile Democrats she has interviewed:

Former President Barry Obama⁠
Then-Vice President Kamala Harris⁠
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ⁠
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries
Elizabeth Warren
Cory Booker
Adam Schiff
Chris Murphy
Jasmine Crockett

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani
Bernie Sanders

And here’s this very same Jennifer Welch targeting our current vice president for assassination, and using two methods, signaling her desire to see him murdered. First, she dehumanizes him as a “white supremacist,” the “Antichrist,” and a “sociopath” who is “not fit to be a father.”

Second, she declaratively calls for “pistols firing at all time [sic] towards this guy.”

Watch for yourself:

Now he wants to be the leader of the white supremacist party, and he has a Usha and four kids problem. But what does he do? He just sits there in a roundabout way all day, every day [and] demeans people with brown skin. And he thinks you’re stupid. Maybe MAGA, is I don’t know. But the coolest thing about JD Vance is that at some point, he wasn’t this white nationalist prostitute bigot… But he came out a complete Antichrist-style sociopath… JD Vance thinks two years from now he’s gonna be president of the United States. and we need to keep firing — pistols firing at all time [sic] towards this guy because he is not fit to be a father, he’s not fit to be a husband, he’s not fit to be vice president. He is a failed drag queen and a pathological liar to his core.

This is what Democrats do, and they do it with the full support of the corporate media.

Welch appears to be desperately calling for some mentally unstable leftist to murder JD Vance, to assassinate the sitting vice president, to gun down a husband and father of four, and to do it before it’s too late, before the “Antichrist” becomes president.

news.title: Georgia on Democrats’ minds: Powering up the Black vote to counter Trump's meddling
news.text:
The Sunday service at Atlanta’s historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, where the late Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. was a senior pastor, is picking up steam, with the congregation punctuating their assent to the preachers and speakers on the pulpit with fervent “Yeahs!”, robust “Okays!” and the occasional “Amens!”

The church on Auburn Avenue in the US National Historic Landmark District of Sweet Auburn in western Atlanta has been at the forefront of African American socio-political engagement. Its preachers voiced visions of equality during the racially segregated era in the Southern states, provided services – such as education – that were denied to the community, and preached a “social gospel” that fueled the 1960s civil rights movement.

The pulpit-to-politics tradition carries on to this day with the Baptist church’s senior pastor, Rev. Raphael Warnock, who was elected to the US Senate in 2020, becoming the first African American to represent Georgia, and the first Black Democrat from a Southern state, to be elected to the upper house of Congress.

Watch moreUSA: Who is Senator Raphael Warnock?

With just weeks to go before the November 3 midterm elections, this Sunday sees Warnock on a roll as he leads the service.

“Alright, come on up. We need everybody to vote,” he proclaims.

“Yeah!” responds the congregation with a chorus of applause.

“A vote is a kind of prayer, for the world we desire for ourselves – and our children,” Warnock continues in the rhythmic, expressive cadence of southern preachers.

And with that, Georgia’s senator hands over the podium to Marc Morial, head of the National Urban League, a civil rights organisation that has served the Black community since 1910.

“The eyes of the nation are on the state of Georgia,” Morial tells the packed church. “When Georgia elected your pastor as its United States senator in the year 2020, many people across the nation had said that was an impossible feat. It could not be done. But Georgia made history,” he notes.

Democrats have had Georgia on their minds over the past few years as it has flipped from a reliably Republican “red” state to an uneven purple with the growth of liberal, educated suburban communities, including a “brain gain” influx of college-educated Black people returning to thriving Southern metropolises such as Atlanta from the rest of the country. But in order to maintain the hues of blue, Democrats need their traditional voter base to come out and vote.

Two years after Donald Trump won Georgia in the 2024 presidential election, and with the Republicans holding Congress, Democrats also have to stem the tide of legislative attempts to dilute the power of Black voters. As the US heads to the polls in the 2026 midterms, studies and editorials warn that the country is “on the cusp of eviscerating Black power”.

Six decades ago, the Ebenezer Baptist Church’s star preacher, Dr. King, launched a civil disobedience campaign to grant African Americans in the southern states their fundamental constitutional right to vote resulting in the landmark 1965 Right to Vote Act. The struggle has changed, but not ended, and Georgia is on the frontlines of the battle. It’s also a fight that has, once again, been largely left to the community to shoulder.

‘Jim Crow in the 21st century’

At the C.T. Martin Natatorium and Recreation Center in Adamsville, a predominantly Black neighbourhood in western Atlanta, early voting kicked off on October 13 in the spacious gymnasium serving as a polling station. A steady stream of voters lined up along walls plastered with election information and warnings such as, “It is illegal to carry a firearm”, into polling stations. Georgia’s early voting slot in the 2026 midterms runs from October 13-30, leaving the last weekend before the November 3 election day free of voting activity.

Outside, in the parking lot of the sprawling premises, a DJ belted out soul music in what was billed as a “get out the vote party”. On the sun-drenched lawn, the hosts of a community collective podcast interviewed politicians, activists and local celebrities emerging from the polling station with “I voted” stickers. At another stall, Deborah Scott, head of Georgia Stand Up, a grassroots NGO, hands out bottles of water, cookies and flyers with voting information.

“Democracy is on the line. And in this democracy fight, it's all going to start and end right here in Georgia,” she says with an infectious smile. “Georgia is going to show the rest of the country that when you organise, mobilise and work with the Black community, you can actually win. Even if they're underfunding it, even if they're not showing us love, we will show our people love.”

“Get out the vote” campaigns are strictly non-partisan initiatives where volunteers abstain from mentioning political parties and preferences.

In Scott’s case, the “love” – or lack of it – refers to a law, the 2021 Election Integrity Act, originally called the Georgia Senate Bill 202, and frequently called “SB 202” across the state.

The act was signed into law by Georgia’s Republican Governor Brian Kemp the year after the state elected two charismatic Democratic senators – Warnock and “Star of the South” Jon Ossoff – to the US Senate, and voted for Joe Biden in presidential race in 2020. Republicans say the law makes it “easier for citizens to vote and harder for anyone to cheat”. From the White House, Biden described it as “Jim Crow in the 21st century”, referring to the racial segregation laws in the southern states before the 1960s civil rights movement.

The law has been the subject of legal challenges by civil rights groups and many court rulings by justices attempting a compromise. Shortly after it passed, the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Georgia alleging that the law is racially discriminatory. But in March 2025, two months after Trump took office for a second term, the Justice Department dropped the lawsuit, stating that it falsely accused Georgia of intentionally suppressing Black votes.

Among its many sections, the law prohibits the handing out of food and water to voters standing in line within 150 feet of a polling station. Scott believes the measure disproportionately affects minority communities. “SB 202 discriminates against black and brown people because only black and brown people were giving water to people who were waiting in lines. Our lines were longer than any other community. People were waiting in lines five, six, ten hours and they could not vote. People were passing out. We couldn't even give them a chair,” she said.

At the C.T. Center, the “get out the vote” party is safely 150 feet away from the polling rooms, but in smaller stations in densely populated neighbourhoods, it presents a challenge, says Scott. “They did that because they don't want democracy. We want democracy. So we said we're still going to do it, we're just going to do it further away. We want people to come and get their water and information before they even get in line,” she explains.

The shadow of 2020

Getting out the vote is critical to Republicans and Democrats in Georgia, a state that went for Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024.

After his 2020 defeat to Biden, Trump falsely claimed he won Georgia even after three vote recounts showed the Republican candidate had lost to Biden by 11,779 votes.

The state was under the media spotlight after Trump made an extraordinary phone call to Georgia’s secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, a Republican. The transcript of the call, which was leaked to the press, showed Trump ordering Raffensperger to “find” enough votes to hand him Georgia. Raffensperger declined.

Six years later, the impact of the Georgia alleged meddling case continues to resonate on the 2026 midterms campaign trail. In February, the FBI raided election offices in the state’s battleground Fulton County to seize sensitive voting records from 2020 in what critics called an unprecedented “instance of the federal government directly interfering in a state election”.

Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in November, was quick to slam the raid. During a visit to an Atlanta Black church, the Democratic “Star of the South” accused Trump of ordering the raid to suppress the Black vote. “The power of Black voters, and the fact that the power of Black voters ejected him from office, may outrage him more than the defeat itself. And so he tries to delegitimise your exercise of power. With elections approaching, he tries to suppress it,” said Ossoff.

Watch moreMidterms 2026: Georgia's Ossof-Collins showdown lies at the heart of the battle for US Senate

Gerrymandering battlefield lines

The suppression of the Black vote has a long history in the American South, particularly in the “Deep South”, the subregion of Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina, that has a distinct historic and cultural identity.

In Georgia, African Americans make up around 30% of the state’s estimated 11 million population, comprising a critical Democratic vote base. “For any Democratic candidate running for office, given the fact that Blacks are overwhelmingly Democratic in their partisan orientation, they absolutely need high voter turnout amongst African American voters – assuming that they vote predictably Democratic – in order to really have a chance at being able to win office,” explained Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at the Atlanta-based Emory University.

But over the past few years, there has been a concerted Republican push, spearheaded by Trump, to redraw congressional districts. Last year, Trump pressed Texas legislators to pass new districting maps to gain more seats for the Republicans in the House of Representatives, where the GOP holds a narrow 220-215 majority. In April, the US Supreme Court, in a landmark ruling, struck down a majority Black congressional district in Louisiana, opening the door for more redistricting and prompting three Southern states to draw new maps.

A Bloomberg News study of congressional maps, published on October 20, found that the gerrymandering – or manipulation of electoral district boundaries to give one political party an unfair electoral advantage – “are having an outsized impact on Black voters, who are more likely to have been shifted into new congressional districts in order to create more safe seats for Republicans ahead of the US midterm elections”.

In Georgia, Republicans in the state legislature earlier this year attempted to follow the Deep South states of Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee in redrawing congressional maps. But the plan was shelved ahead of the November midterms for fear of a voter backlash against the party.

Standing on the C.T. Center lawn after casting her ballot, Shirley Clarke Franklin, a former Atlanta mayor and a veteran Democrat, credited Georgia’s progressive politicians for the pushback. “African Americans in Georgia, especially our leadership, stood up against redistricting when it was raised in our legislature. And our legislature, which is dominated by the party that wanted to do redistricting, backed down,” said Franklin, referring to state Republicans. “So, the organisational skills of Georgians, the history of fighting for our rights, serves us well in difficult times.”

The pushback may have succeeded for the moment, but analysts believe Republicans will attempt to put the issue back on the agenda after the midterms.

Gillespie notes that this year’s gubernatorial race between Republican billionaire Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms to replace Republican Governor Kemp – whose term ends in January 2027 – could play a key role.

“Redistricting is definitely not off the table,” says Gillespie. “The timing of it will depend on who becomes governor of Georgia. It's highly likely that the governor [Republican Brian Kemp] will call a special session in November or December to address redistricting so that he can sign that into law if Keisha Lance Bottoms wins and before a new legislature comes in [in January 2027]. There might be less urgency to do that if Rick Jackson is elected governor.”

The ‘gift’ of the vote

Cruising westward on Atlanta’s Martin Luther King Jr. Drive in a car loaded with cartons of his self-published book, “All Power Back to the People,” Scotty Smart is upbeat about the power of his vote.

“If we vote in this election, we have the ability to fight back and slow down some of the things that are happening across the country,” says the young Black activist.

But minutes later, Smart bristles when asked about the Black male vote for Trump in 2024. “That's a false narrative put out by certain media platforms that like to chastise Black men,” he maintains. “In 2024, Black men overwhelmingly voted Democrat. But the emphasis is always put on that one small demographic.”

He has a point. A Pew Research Center voter analysis found that approximately 77% of Black men voted for Kamala Harris, while 21% voted for Trump. Among Black women, approximately 92% supported Harris, and 7% supported Trump.

After two years of Trump’s second presidency and the Iran war exacerbating the cost of living crisis, Smart believes the Black vote will overwhelmingly stick with the Democrats in the midterms. “Truckers are ready to go on strike because the diesel prices are so high, people are upset because food is so expensive. It's gotten so bad that people are finally seeing the effects” of Trump’s policies, he notes.

Standing outside the Ebenezer at the end of the Sunday service, Kamilah Aminah Jones, a psychotherapist and licensed ecclesiastical minister at the historic church, chokes up as she draws from the past to explain her responsibility, as a citizen, to vote in the latest elections.

“It's a gift. It's really a gift. And I'm getting emotional,” she pauses briefly to collect herself before continuing. “I'm getting emotional just thinking about that … It’s a promise that my ancestors possibly prayed for, not just prayed for, there was blood, sweat and tears to have that opportunity. And I stand in that now. I have a voice. It's something I can never take for granted.”
news.summary: President Donald Trump's push to redistrict congressional maps and a Georgia state election law disproportionately affecting African Americans are aimed at diluting the power of the Black vote. Six decades after Atlanta was at the heart of the civil rights movement that granted Blacks in the southern states the right to vote, the community is fighting back.
news.author: Leela Jacinto

news.title: Elon Musk Blows Fuse Over Calls For Potential Investigations Into Him: 'I Will Find Out'
news.text:
Tech trillionaire Elon Musk appeared concerned on Wednesday about burgeoning calls for lawmakers to investigate him should Democrats flip the House or Senate in the upcoming midterms, reacting on social media to reports and critics with varying levels of ire.

He seemed particularly troubled by a new Politico report titled “Capitol Agenda: Dem Gavels Are Coming for Elon Musk,” on House Democrats in their purported quest to investigate Musk over his time as head of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency or DOGE.

“Live by the sword, die by the sword,” Musk wrote Wednesday on X while resharing the article. “Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets …”

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spearheaded DOGE under President Donald Trump in a stated effort to slash wasteful public spending, only to dismantle numerous key agencies, including the Department of Education and USAID, which administered civilian foreign aid.

Musk, whose companies receive billions in federal contracts, has also been accused of using DOGE to gut regulatory agencies that were investigating his businesses. The X owner seemed irate Wednesday at the notion, according to tech journalist Kara Swisher.

He commented on a clip of her remarks, “Sounds like Swisher really wants to go to prison.”

Swisher argued during an appearance on The Bulwark podcast “Receipts” that Musk would already be in jail if former Vice President Kamala Harris won the 2024 election, warning “if Donald Trump loses the House and the Senate, I would worry … no matter how rich he is.”

She added, “There were all these agencies, some of which he put a knife in and killed in the DOGE, many of whom were investigating him. He stopped like half a dozen investigations of his various companies. So they’re gonna start investigating again. You think he’s not on the list?”

Swisher continued, “He’s at the top of that list. Donald Trump obviously is at the top, and his family ... but Elon Musk is right up there for that ... He knows what’s coming. Like, he’s not stupid. Of all the many things you can say about him is he has a very big sense of fate.”

She concluded, “And I think it’s coming for him. And real hard.”

The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that Musk last week personally ordered his network of Starlink satellites slowed in Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing invasion there, and Democrats have kept an eye on his potentially unconstitutional actions at DOGE.

Musk has claimed that the military version of Starlink being used in the region is solely owned and operated by the U.S. government, and that any “limits on speed or usage” are decided by the military “and ultimately POTUS,” meaning Trump.

While it remains to be seen if the world’s richest man will face actual investigations following the midterms, Musk seemingly reacted to the Journal story Wednesday by writing on X, “Some fools still think the legacy news is real. Amazing.”

The article’s co-author, Alex Ward, responded on X, writing, “Sir, is this your comment to our story?”

news.title: Democrats are raising far more money than Republicans in the US midterms campaign – here’s why that matters
news.text:
For anyone even remotely interested in US politics, the midterm elections are the only game in town at the moment. In fact, there has already been plenty of ink spilled about what a “blue wave” landslide for the Democrats might mean for Trump and Trumpism – and how likely that outcome even is.

If polling is anything to go by, prospects are looking increasingly grim for the Republicans. But I want to take a minute to point to a secondary data source which supports this – money.

The Republicans, to quote Politico, are getting completely “smoked” when it comes to fundraising for the midterms. Their candidates – in red states and blue – are raising significantly less cash than the Democrats.

This simply means the Democrats have been able to spend far more money on their campaigns than Republicans. According to the Federal Election Commission, which publishes data on fundraising and spending, candidates have spent about US$2.85 billion (£2.12 billion) in this election cycle. And the big spenders have pretty much all been Democrats.

This matters. There’s a whole lot that we don’t know about money in politics, but there’s also a decent amount we do. One thing we know, is that money matters for electoral outcomes. That doesn’t mean those that spend more money will necessarily win an election – just ask Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, both of whom raised significantly more money than Donald Trump, but still lost. But candidates need to spend a certain amount of cash (think of it like a start-up cost) to stand a chance in the first place.

As the Clinton and Harris examples show, having (and spending) a huge war chest doesn’t guarantee victory. But in donor-led democracies like the USA and the UK, the ability to raise money is tied to, and tells us something about, electoral prospects. People don’t tend to give money to candidates they don’t see as having a realistic prospect of winning – you wouldn’t bet on a donkey to win the Kentucky Derby.

We saw an example of this during the UK 2024 general election. The Conservatives, to borrow the American phrase, were getting smoked by Labour when it came to raising money prior to the election. In fact, pre-poll donations to the Tories fell by 90% between 2019 and 2024. People didn’t think they were going to win, and they were right, so they kept their hands in their pockets.

When the Financial Times asked some Tory donors why this might be, they revealed another thing we know about money in politics: that most donors do want something in return for the money they give. “Any self-respecting businessperson conducts due diligence before an investment decision,” said one donor. “Time will tell whether the smart money will back Mr Sunak.” It didn’t.

We are seeing this story playing out again in the 2026 US midterms. It seems the smart money in the US is looking at the price of diesel, looking at the general sense of chaos engulfing the Trump administration and, most importantly, looking at Donald Trump’s catastrophic approval ratings – and sitting this one out.

The Republicans aren’t broke

But that’s not the full story. While Democratic candidates are out-raising their Republican rivals by five to one from donations, Republicans are bringing in more than Democrats from outside groups. These are political action committees (PACs) and super-PACs.

But this is partisan money, not smart money – it’s cash generated by each side’s political machine, most of which can’t be committed to supporting individual candidates due to the complexities of US campaign finance laws. So it tells us far less about electoral prospects.

Elon Musk, for example, is the primary funder of Texas PAC which has spent US$131 million attacking James Talarico, the Senate candidate for the Democrats in Texas. He gave a further US$158m to the general Republican Senate Super PAC in the last financial quarter too.

So let’s not kid ourselves that the Republicans are suddenly electoral paupers. The Texas spending alone is far more than all spending, from all parties, at the 2024 general election in the UK.

Money talks

This, of course, speaks volumes about US politics, and is something that should cause concern in other democracies that choose not to place upper limits on donations or spending. Since a 2010 Supreme Court case known as Citizens United (which ruled that the first amendment protecting freedom of speech also applied to political donations), spending in the US – particularly from PACs and Super PACs – has ballooned exponentially.

All the while the pool of donors has got smaller. Figures from the 2024 presidential election cycle are pretty stark on this. In 2008, mega-donors – classified as those that give over US$1 million – made up just 4% of Republican funders. By 2024 that figure was 56%.

It is widely agreed that for elections to have integrity they should embody principles of fair participation, deliberation, contestation and adjudication. All of these are undermined by a system of political financing like this. Or, put differently, speech isn’t all that free if everyone’s trying to talk and a crazy guy with a megaphone drowns them out.

The lesson I draw from this for the UK is that creating an oligarchic state where a few parties are largely, if not entirely, propped up by the world’s richest men is not a massively healthy sign of functioning democracy. Or, as I put it to the New York Times last week: “We kind of point to the US as a system of worst practices.”

What does this tell us about US politics in 2026? Well, the smart money is saying the Republicans are in for a thrashing. But this is an America where a smart approach to money in politics left the building a long time ago. And the rest of us – especially in the UK – could learn an awful lot from that too.

news.title: Elon Musk threatens to jail Hillary Clinton's podcast partner after her election warning
news.text:
A panicked Elon Musk threatened Hillary Clinton's podcast partner with prison time after she issued a post-election threat against him.

Kara Swisher became the target of Musk's ire after she appeared on The Bulwark and said she claimed to know "what's coming for him" should a "blue wave" victory grace Democrats come Nov. 3, the day of the midterm elections.

Swisher suggested that Democrats should investigate Musk if they gain control of both congressional chambers and even went so far as to say Musk would already be in jail had former Vice President Kamala Harris won the 2024 presidential election.
