"Under Kamala Harris, he might be in jail right now, right?" she suggested. "And that's not because she's some avenging fury. It's because there is a lot of questions around different companies of his."

Swisher, who launched the High Stakes podcast with Hillary Clinton last week, went on to claim that the agencies affected by Musk's cuts when he headed the Department of Government Efficiency would have been the first to investigate his companies - which include Tesla and SpaceX.

"If Donald Trump loses the Senate, I would be worried, if I were him, even though how rich he is. He has a very big sense of fate. And I think it's coming for him. And real hard," she said.

A furious Musk took to his social media platform, X, shortly after the podcast episode aired, slamming the tech journalist's comments.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword. Sounds like Swisher really wants to go to prison," he wrote.

In a separate post, he added, "Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets."

Earlier this week, Musk was accused of attempting to "buy Texas" after pouring millions of dollars into Republican Ken Paxton's campaign.

"Ken Paxton is funded by one dude. Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants his very own, personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas," Talarico said.

"Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat in Texas. We just found out that he is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate and defeat this movement we built in our state," he added.

"In all likelihood, if you have seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon," he continued. "If you've gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you've received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too."

Musk reportedly poured record-breaking amounts of money into the midterm elections this year, hoping to save Republicans from a wipeout.

The tech mogul has already donated an astounding $366 million to groups backing GOP candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, The New York Times reported.

That is roughly $76 million more than the $290 million the world's richest man invested to help elect President Donald Trump in 2024.

Sources familiar with Musk's fundraising efforts told the NYT that his donations are among the largest in U.S. history, with him having given even more in undisclosed contributions over the past two election cycles.

Recipients of Musk's money include the Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, his own America PAC, the Republican Governors Association, and the Republican Attorneys General Association. He's also given money to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton.

Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC, told The Daily Beast that the country could become "socialist, woke, and borderless" if Democrats win next month.

"If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke, and borderless country," he said.

"These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history," he added.

The comments refer to pre-midterm polling that shows Democrats leading by up to 9 points on the generic congressional ballot, with previously safe Republican seats in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina now competitive.

Democrats' momentum can largely be attributed to Trump's poor approval ratings, which are driven by the war against Iran and the widespread unaffordability it's caused - which he dismissed as a "hoax" despite overwhelming evidence.

news.title: Democrats are raising far more money than Republicans in the US midterms campaign – here’s why that matters
news.text:
For anyone even remotely interested in US politics, the midterm elections are the only game in town at the moment. In fact, there has already been plenty of ink spilled about what a “blue wave” landslide for the Democrats might mean for Trump and Trumpism – and how likely that outcome even is. 

If polling is anything to go by, prospects are looking increasingly grim for the Republicans. But I want to take a minute to point to a secondary data source which supports this – money.

The Republicans, to quote Politico, are getting completely “smoked” when it comes to fundraising for the midterms. Their candidates – in red states and blue – are raising significantly less cash than the Democrats.

This simply means the Democrats have been able to spend far more money on their campaigns than Republicans. According to the Federal Election Commission, which publishes data on fundraising and spending, candidates have spent about US$2.85 billion (£2.12 billion) in this election cycle. And the big spenders have pretty much all been Democrats. 

This matters. There’s a whole lot that we don’t know about money in politics, but there’s also a decent amount we do. One thing we know, is that money matters for electoral outcomes. That doesn’t mean those that spend more money will necessarily win an election – just ask Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, both of whom raised significantly more money than Donald Trump, but still lost. But candidates need to spend a certain amount of cash (think of it like a start-up cost) to stand a chance in the first place. 

As the Clinton and Harris examples show, having (and spending) a huge war chest doesn’t guarantee victory. But in donor-led democracies like the USA and the UK, the ability to raise money is tied to, and tells us something about, electoral prospects. People don’t tend to give money to candidates they don’t see as having a realistic prospect of winning – you wouldn’t bet on a donkey to win the Kentucky Derby.

We saw an example of this during the UK 2024 general election. The Conservatives, to borrow the American phrase, were getting smoked by Labour when it came to raising money prior to the election. In fact, pre-poll donations to the Tories fell by 90% between 2019 and 2024. People didn’t think they were going to win, and they were right, so they kept their hands in their pockets. 

When the Financial Times asked some Tory donors why this might be, they revealed another thing we know about money in politics: that most donors do want something in return for the money they give. “Any self-respecting businessperson conducts due diligence before an investment decision,” said one donor. “Time will tell whether the smart money will back Mr Sunak.” It didn’t.

We are seeing this story playing out again in the 2026 US midterms. It seems the smart money in the US is looking at the price of diesel, looking at the general sense of chaos engulfing the Trump administration and, most importantly, looking at Donald Trump’s catastrophic approval ratings – and sitting this one out. 

The Republicans aren’t broke

But that’s not the full story. While Democratic candidates are out-raising their Republican rivals by five to one from donations, Republicans are bringing in more than Democrats from outside groups. These are political action committees (PACs) and super-PACs. 

But this is partisan money, not smart money – it’s cash generated by each side’s political machine, most of which can’t be committed to supporting individual candidates due to the complexities of US campaign finance laws. So it tells us far less about electoral prospects.

Elon Musk, for example, is the primary funder of Texas PAC which has spent US$131 million attacking James Talarico, the Senate candidate for the Democrats in Texas. He gave a further US$158m to the general Republican Senate Super PAC in the last financial quarter too. 

So let’s not kid ourselves that the Republicans are suddenly electoral paupers. The Texas spending alone is far more than all spending, from all parties, at the 2024 general election in the UK.

Money talks

This, of course, speaks volumes about US politics, and is something that should cause concern in other democracies that choose not to place upper limits on donations or spending. Since a 2010 Supreme Court case known as Citizens United (which ruled that the first amendment protecting freedom of speech also applied to political donations), spending in the US – particularly from PACs and Super PACs – has ballooned exponentially. 

All the while the pool of donors has got smaller. Figures from the 2024 presidential election cycle are pretty stark on this. In 2008, mega-donors – classified as those that give over US$1 million – made up just 4% of Republican funders. By 2024 that figure was 56%. 

It is widely agreed that for elections to have integrity they should embody principles of fair participation, deliberation, contestation and adjudication. All of these are undermined by a system of political financing like this. Or, put differently, speech isn’t all that free if everyone’s trying to talk and a crazy guy with a megaphone drowns them out.

The lesson I draw from this for the UK is that creating an oligarchic state where a few parties are largely, if not entirely, propped up by the world’s richest men is not a massively healthy sign of functioning democracy. Or, as I put it to the New York Times last week: “We kind of point to the US as a system of worst practices.” 

What does this tell us about US politics in 2026? Well, the smart money is saying the Republicans are in for a thrashing. But this is an America where a smart approach to money in politics left the building a long time ago. And the rest of us – especially in the UK – could learn an awful lot from that too.
news.summary: History tells us that money talks when it comes to US elections. Regardless of who you support, this can’t be good for democracy.

news.title: Kamala’s voter-roll freakout hits blue states hard
news.text:
Kamala Harris has made election integrity a big talking point ahead of the midterms. The former vice president’s latest claims of cheating raise an obvious question: Does she object to voter-roll maintenance itself, or can she identify a lawful safeguard she actually supports?

At an appearance in South Korea last week, the former vice president alleged “overt cheating” in American elections, citing voter-roll purges. In September, she accused officials of “cheating by purging voter rolls.” Over the summer, she also criticized the SAVE America Act for requiring documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections.

Harris can keep calling voter-roll purges ‘cheating.’ But California’s unanswered questions and New Jersey’s documented registration failure demand more than talking points.

Harris wants to turn basic election safeguards into the boogeyman of election administration. But isn’t the point to ensure that only American citizens vote in our elections?

Election officials must not improperly remove eligible voters. They also have an obligation to identify ineligible registrations. Harris talks about purges without making that distinction. Americans deserve to know which safeguards she opposes and why.

Start with California, Harris’ home state. On Monday, the Justice Department charged 28 lawful permanent residents with federal election-related offenses, including fraudulent registration and illegal voting. Eleven were arrested. The charges are allegations, not convictions, but the cases warrant serious attention.

Federal prosecutors say all 28 appeared on a list of more than 20,000 people the government believes are likely noncitizens registered in California. The Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security sued the state on October 15, seeking to stop ballots attributed to people on that list from being counted until their citizenship is verified.

Governor Gavin Newsom (D) called the lawsuit an attempt to “suppress California voters.” The state should be able to show how it verifies eligibility and corrects its rolls.

It cannot. A separate public records response exposes an accounting problem: California’s statewide voter-registration system “does not contain a voter status reason for cancellation due to non-citizenship.” The state could not provide a count of registrations canceled for that specific reason. Why not?

New Jersey supplies an even clearer example of why verification cannot be an afterthought. In July, Governor Mikie Sherrill (D) acknowledged that a “serious software error” had registered approximately 6,600 people who answered “no” when asked whether they were U.S. citizens during motor vehicle transactions. The “error” occurred between June 2023 and June 2024.

RELATED: California makes ‘massive concession’ in lawsuit over 20,000 'likely noncitizen' voters, DOJ says

 CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP/Getty Images

A subsequent state accounting found that about 340 newly registered people had actually voted. New Jersey claims it has no evidence that those votes changed an election result. That does not excuse a system that registered people after they expressly declined to attest to citizenship.

At a House Judiciary hearing in September, I noted that at least three New Jersey elections in 2025 were decided by a single vote or ended in a tie. When a race is that close, election officials cannot shrug off registration errors.

New Jersey voters understand the stakes. A Rutgers-Eagleton poll released this month found that 82% of state residents support requiring photo ID to vote in person, while 71% favor documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register.

Even Sherrill has expressed support for voter ID. That requirement establishes identity; proof of citizenship establishes eligibility. They serve different purposes, and neither question should be brushed aside with a slogan about voter suppression.

RELATED: ‘DON'T TRUST THE POLLS’: Failed Democratic candidate melts down after ANOTHER pollster outed as a total fake

 Katie McTiernan/Anadolu/Getty Images

Minnesota has its own lesson in the need for clear rules. Governor Tim Walz (D) signed a 2023 law that lets residents get standard driver’s licenses without proving lawful immigration status. During an October 2025 legislative hearing, state Rep. Patti Anderson (R) pressed state elections director Paul Linnell on whether those licenses could be used as voter identification. He failed to give a direct yes-or-no answer.

Minnesota does permit a driver’s license as proof of residence for Election Day registration. Citizenship eligibility is a separate requirement. Election officials should be able to explain the distinction simply, especially when lawmakers ask about vulnerabilities.

Accurate voter rolls, citizenship verification, and clear identity rules protect the votes of eligible Americans. Officials should explain how those safeguards work and correct failures when they find them.

Harris can keep calling voter-roll purges “cheating.” But California’s unanswered questions and New Jersey’s documented registration failure demand more than talking points. If she believes these safeguards are improper, she should explain which ones — and what she would do instead.

news.title: Islamophobia is getting louder. Why isn’t the response?
news.text:
Welcome to The Midterms, Actually. Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. Let’s get into it.
One thing I’m thinking about: Electability and identity are intertwined 
On Sunday, former President Barack Obama did something most others seemed to avoid: He called out the Trump administration’s targeting of Rep. Ilhan Omar.
The administration, Obama wrote, is “actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar” over a theory he called unsubstantiated: that she was 18, not 17, when her father was naturalized. The effort, he said, “should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views.” 
The statement stands in contrast to the mixed response of Democrats on the campaign trail and the relative silence of the mainstream press. House leadership put out a statement condemning the raid — but there’s been nothing from Senate Democratic leadership and little from the crop of elected officials expected to run for president in 2028. 
As The Intercept’s Adam Johnson pointed out, the August 2025 raid on former Trump adviser John Bolton drew scathing editorials from the New York Times, Washington Post, and the Wall Street Journal within days. The same goes for other ways Trump has weaponized the federal government against his political enemies, from the cases against James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James to the pursuit of Federal Reserve officials (Obama named all three in his statement). Omar’s raid has drawn much less intense coverage. Last week, I got three requests from cable outlets to discuss “news of the day” — each mentioned fired White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, new midterms polling, and some combination of Pete Hegseth and the war with Iran. None mentioned Omar. 
The entire episode has reminded me of Trump’s targeting of Black journalists like Don Lemon and Georgia Fort. Earlier this year, they were indicted after covering an anti-ICE protest that disrupted a service at Cities Church in St. Paul, and both have pleaded not guilty. In that case, there was also a muted reaction from the establishment press, possibly because of mixed feelings about Lemon personally or the lack of solidarity with independent Black media. Still, that silence was shortsighted, as the Trump administration used the incident as a stepping stone to target the wider media apparatus (See: Trump’s September attempt to bar CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House).
With that in mind, I don’t think it’s hard to guess why Omar hasn’t received the fulsome backing of her party. I don’t think it’s the merits of the case: She hasn’t been charged with a crime, and the theory depends on a decades-old immigration filing by a father who died in 2020. It’s likely the fact that the Minnesota progressive has herself had a tense relationship with the Democratic establishment. That dates back to the 2019 fight over comments Omar made about the influence of the pro-Israel lobby in Congress, which some took to be antisemitic. In recent weeks, Minnesota Democrats, including Rep. Angie Craig and Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s office, criticized Omar’s plans to appear at an October 26 event hosted by state Sen. Omar Fateh with Hasan Piker, the controversial leftist Twitch streamer who has become a lightning rod in this year’s primaries.
But there’s another factor that we should also name in this episode: Islamophobia. As I discussed with Mehdi Hasan on Substack Live a couple weeks ago, the rise of the progressive left cannot be untangled from Muslim elected officials who have become its face: Omar in Minnesota, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, and Zohran Mamdani in New York City. And in each case, these candidates have faced attacks that explicitly seek to frame their religion and identity as inherently anti-American, a threat not only to our national values but our democracy itself.
Asked on CBS whether he believed El-Sayed was a terrorist, Republican Mike Rogers said to “look at the data — it’s pretty clear.” In a recent television ad (a seven-figure buy titled “Threat”) launched by Rogers and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, its narrator says, “Abdul raises money from dangerous people who finance terrorist networks,” tying the candidate to the Muslim Brotherhood and al-Qaeda. The NRSC’s ads also notably use his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.
But importantly, it’s not just Republicans engaging in overt bigotry. They have also been aided by moderate Democrats and the press, who have used the guise of “electability” to beat the same drum. Think back to the New York City mayoral race, where (Democrat!) Andrew Cuomo spent the final weeks running a campaign virtually indistinguishable from the tactics of the MAGA right. On a radio show, host Sid Rosenberg said Mamdani would cheer if another 9/11 happened, and Cuomo laughed, seeming to agree. Cuomo’s X account even posted, then deleted, an AI-generated ad called “Criminals for Zohran Mamdani,” which opens with a fake Mamdani eating rice with his hands. The campaign blamed a “junior staffer.”
The worst part: In following Republicans down the road of interrogating the Scary Muslims, we perpetrate a form of hate that has real costs. Just this May, two teenagers opened fire at the Islamic Center of San Diego, killing three people, and left behind a manifesto invoking the Christchurch mosque shooter. Analysts at the Anti-Defamation League found it expressed sweeping hatred of Muslims, Jews, Black and Hispanic people, and the LGBTQ+ community.
And journalistically, we avoid a more nuanced conversation that is the one worth having: the connection between identity and electability. The discussion about candidates El-Sayed and Mamdani, to this point, has focused on whether their progressive policy stances can play well in a general election. However, research shows that while candidates of marginalized backgrounds (women, Black and Latinos, Arabs, etc.) face an electoral penalty from voters regardless of ideology or political party, that’s especially true for Muslim candidates. A study of state legislative races in Politics and Religion this year found Muslim candidates were roughly 16 percentage points less likely to win general elections than non-Muslim candidates, and 10–15 points behind other racial minorities. Experiments by the political scientist Nazita Lajevardi, cited in that paper, found voters about 10 percent less likely to pick a Muslim candidate over a white one, with religion rather than race as the trigger.
This would seem to explain some of the reason El-Sayed seems to be running behind other Senate Democrats (if we believe the polling). But you rarely hear that reasoning given by the electability crowd, who more than often cites his progressive beliefs, and are we just supposed to nominate Christian white guys forever?
Here’s what is undeniable: Republicans have become quite adept at putting minority communities against each other in the Trump era, and they’re running that playbook in Michigan. Whether it’s telling Black communities that emerging immigrant populations are taking their jobs or telling immigrant communities that Democrats are too focused on Black issues, the strategy has been to exploit the racial tension at the heart of the Democratic base. And to some degree — it’s working.
In an August interview with Clay Cane at The Grio, a Black-focused outlet, El-Sayed said “mistrust among Black folk in Metro Detroit is well-founded,” pointing to what he described as tensions between some Arab and Muslim business owners. And the skepticism runs the other way too — as part of the difficulty El-Sayed has faced in Black communities is tied to the Islamophobia among that voting block. One example: At a July campaign event for Haley Stevens, a Farmington school board trustee told a Michigan Chronicle reporter, “Don’t just come in here speaking Arabic,” remarks the Council on American Islamic Relations condemned as anti-Arab racism and many read as aimed at El-Sayed. At an August 19 press conference, an older Black man in Detroit shouted at El-Sayed, “He’s an Arab — he don’t care nothing about Black folks.”
The layered nature of this issue should not be hard to grasp. Ask liberals about the 2024 election, and they are quick to point out the racism and sexism faced by candidates like Kamala Harris, and rightly argue that impacted her “electability” just as much as her refusal to break from President Joe Biden or embrace a clear ideological lane. But they conveniently leave out the importance of identity when it comes to Omar, El-Sayed, Mamdani, or even candidates like Francesca Hong in Wisconsin or Angie Nixon in Florida. As Zaid Jilani wrote recently, establishment Democrats are “effectively denying that prejudice exists in the United States if they’re really going to argue that Abdul El-Sayed will perform a few points behind other Democrats because of his PolIcY ViEwS rather than the GOP hating Muslims for 25 years.”
But we should be clear: “Hating Muslims” is not a prejudice that’s limited to the GOP, just as issues like racism, sexism, or antisemitism aren’t housed on one side of the aisle either. And in selectively ignoring the central role that prejudice plays in electoral politics — yes, even with progressive candidates — electability-focused Democrats aid the GOP’s desire to sow discord among their base.
The main reason for Democrats to stand up for Omar or El-Sayed is because it’s right, and they, too, have a place in American democracy. But at minimum, Democrats should see that in ignoring explicit Islamophobia — on the campaign trail or in the White House — they are being rather shortsighted. Trump’s campaign of retribution is unlikely to spare any enemy. Muslims may be the focus right now. But there’s no telling who’s next. You’re either for a multiracial, multifaith coalition — or you’re not.
One thing I’m hearing 
This week, we talked to Christian Paz, a Vox correspondent covering national politics and American religion. He’s been reporting from Kansas for an upcoming story on pastor and Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton, whose race has emerged as a major campaign battleground in the final stretch. I wanted to ask him how Hamilton’s faith is shaping his campaign, what he is hearing from voters, and what the race could tell us about the Democrats’ ability to compete in long held Republican states. 
How is Adam Hamilton’s background as a pastor shaping his pitch, and what is he doing differently from other Democrats?
Watching Hamilton on the trail, it was remarkable to me how much his Methodist faith was at the heart of everything he talked about: about healthcare, climate, immigration, and foreign policy, about how his personal views either conflict with or bolster his policy stance, about how Trump and the GOP have failed Kansans, and about why he even decided to run (after he spent time dwelling on the Sermon on the Mount). He tailors his stump speech to different audiences, of course: At a progressive book shop, he leaned into a more anti-Trump speech; at a senior center he talked up his more conservative viewpoints on immigration and climate; at a Republicans for Hamilton rally he talked about the political center and why he wants to build a big tent; at a chapel, he led the audience in singing a hymn and quoted extensively from the Gospels as he shared his personally “pro-life” views — but it was all not just tinged, but immersed in Christianity.
It’s something I’ve only seen people like Rev. Raphael Warnock do, when speaking at churches on the campaign trail in 2020 and 2021. And it was different from James Talarico too — this guy leads a megachurch, and at times can slip into a kind of evangelical tone. That’s all pretty different than any other Democrat I’ve watched this cycle.
Hamilton needs to win over Kansans outside his party to have a shot. What were you hearing on the ground talking to voters?
The faith pitch is a huge part of why it does seem like he has a shot at winning: It doesn’t seem like he’s adopting or borrowing the language of the faithful, or their aesthetics, to talk politics, or just pitching the political center as a way to persuade voters. It’s that he’s adopting the tone and language of politics to talk about his faith — not the other way around. And the result is that when he talks about building a big tent, holding heterodox views, coexisting with people you disagree with — people trust and believe him.
I think I talked to more actual independents and Republicans who are backing Hamilton than actual die-hard Democrats over the days I was in Kansas. Some of these folks have voted at the local level for Democrats before, but tended to vote Republican at the national level. What unified those conversations was the sense that they think Hamilton is authentic, is a moral man with good character, and seems to be truly independent.
Others, including Democrats, said they appreciated how much time Hamilton spent talking about freedom of religion and diversity of thought — they liked that he would preface his religious talk with assurances that he wasn’t trying to convert anyone or force religion into people’s lives, but would also say he wasn’t going to compromise on it because of how genuinely he believes those things.
What could this race tell us about Democrats’ ability to reach religious voters in other Republican states?
The race already tells us a few things, regardless of who wins or loses: Democrats should be creating opportunities to elevate religious people or clergy who want to run for office. Those who aspire to run for office should also feel more comfortable talking about their faith if it’s actually a part of their lives. And Democrats shouldn’t feel beholden to the secular/atheist/none of the above/nothing in particular segment of their base because that isn’t big enough to actually win elections.

news.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
news.text: Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night. The hour-long showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall â a topic touched on during the debate. Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates. Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. "Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric." Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse. Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation. FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part." Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right' Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week. "And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd. Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda. "No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump. Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports. "Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right." Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate. Both candidates say there are 'two genders' The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are. "There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls." "There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded. TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports. Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females. "I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight." Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology." Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people. Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons. "We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said. But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer. "You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers. Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement. Hamilton pushed back sharply. "This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best." BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster' Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle." The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed. "The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders." "I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.
news.summary: Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton clashed over Trump, transgender athletes and AI in a heated Kansas Senate debate on Wednesday.

news.title: Courts Should Not Micromanage Prisons on Transgender Issues
news.text:
In the most memorable political ad of 2024, Donald Trump pummeled Kamala Harris for pledging taxpayer money for transgender surgeries for prisoners. It was already happening. One of Trump’s Day One executive orders in 2025 told the Bureau of Prisons to put a stop to this. Almost two years into his term, the courts are blocking Trump from changing the policy. They shouldn’t.

The BOP, after spending a year developing a 3,200-page administrative record, issued new regulations in early 2026 barring inmates from access to surgical and hormone therapy treatments or “social accommodations,” such as wigs, breast padding, binders, or makeup, all of which could be confiscated. The policy would grant the affected inmates access only to mental health services and medications such as antidepressants. The BOP cited shifts in the science as well as security and prison-administration concerns.

Transgender surgeries, hormones, and attire are all things that adults are free to choose if they wish. But there are many choices that people lose in prison, where they depend upon the taxpayer to foot the bill and where the security environment can be volatile.

This being a Trump policy, a lawsuit followed. Inmates represented by the American Civil Liberties Union sued, claiming that this policy was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) as well as violating other provisions of federal law and the Constitution. Judge Royce Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted a series of preliminary injunctions against the BOP policy in June and August, and a divided panel of the D.C. Circuit declined to stay the most recent injunction. On Wednesday, in a one-line order without explanation, a 7–2 Supreme Court did the same. Only Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented, also without an opinion.

The sole basis offered by the courts for the injunction is that the agency failed to do its homework under the APA. Judge Lamberth wrote: “It appears clear that the agency had made up its mind with respect to the plaintiffs’ gender-affirming care” in reaching its decision. Two judges of the D.C. Circuit ruled that the policy “is arbitrary and capricious because the [BOP] did not adequately consider its own experience providing gender-affirming care under its prior policy. . . . For example, BOP makes claims about the security impact of providing gender-affirming care without addressing whether such issues have occurred.” This sort of judicial flyspecking of executive policy, after a protracted administrative process, is harmful and especially counterproductive in the prison setting.

The courts ought to restrain the executive branch when it exceeds its authority or violates the law. But this sort of APA review simply second-guesses matters within executive discretion.

Moreover, Judge Justin Walker of the D.C. Circuit raised a serious concern, in dissent, that the strictures of the Prison Litigation Reform Act were violated by Judge Lamberth’s issuing multiple “rolling injunctions” to keep the policy frozen in place for over the statutory 90-day limit on the basis of a preliminary ruling.

The constant stream of emergency applications asking the Supreme Court to rule quickly on half-baked cases is undoubtedly wearying to the justices. Several of them have complained that the Court keeps getting asked to handle stay requests that don’t lend themselves to the kind of deliberative, carefully reasoned work in which the Court takes pride. We sympathize. But so long as district judges are serving the executive branch their own undercooked orders, the Court should send them back.
news.summary: The Supreme Court should have stopped a district judge from enjoining the Bureau of Prisons on transgender services for inmates.

news.title: Roger Marshall-Adam Hamilton debate: The view from Great Bend
news.text:
Great Bend, KS

I watched Wednesday night’s debate between Adam Hamilton and Roger Marshall at Dry Lake Brewing Co., on Main Street in Great Bend, Kansas.

Great Bend is Marshall’s home turf. Kansas’ junior U.S. senator spent decades practicing medicine here before entering politics. But this wasn’t what you’d call a hometown crowd.

The gathering was organized by some of the town’s Democrats, liberals, moderates and disaffected Republicans — locals who aren’t exactly swimming in political company in this deeply conservative part of Kansas.

Roughly half the room was senior citizens. There were also some younger parents, and a few children running around. About 50 people turned up to sip craft beers, nibble on homemade pretzels, and watch the big show on the big screen.

Notes on the debate

Before getting to the crowd’s reactions, I’ll share a few of my own.

Overall, I thought the debate was fairly even. I doubt it changed many minds. Marshall performed a little better than I’d expected. He was certainly more polished than the reports from the Kansas State Fair debate in September and his notorious emergency exit from an Oakley town hall last year would lead you to believe. (Although it does seem that Marshall skipped the post-debate interview.)

It must be said that Roger Marshall was sniffing a lot during this debate. I can’t be the only one who noticed this.Former Kansas U.S. Senator and one-time presidential candidate Bob Dole remains popular, even among Democrats here. Big cheers when Hamilton called Dole “our greatest Republican senator.”

If you’d watched the debate with the sound off, you might have mistaken Marshall for the challenger and Hamilton for the incumbent. Marshall was easily the more aggressive of the two, and by the second question he was pointing his finger at Hamilton as he spoke. Hamilton, characteristically mild-mannered, mostly declined to match his opponent’s intensity.

Marshall relentlessly invoked Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. Marshall seemed determined to make the election a referendum on Schumer, Joe Biden, Kamala Harris, Barack Hussein Obama, and just about any other well-known Democrat whose name he could work into an answer.

At one point, Marshall boasted about working with Sen. Bernie Sanders on health care legislation. A few minutes later, he was warning that Sanders would be in charge of health care if Kansans elected Hamilton and handed Democrats control of the Senate. Is Bernie a valued legislative partner or a dangerous socialist?

I should acknowledge that I missed a few of Hamilton’s retorts, and some of Marshall’s remarks, because of the noise inside Dry Lake Brewing Co. Marshall’s answers drew several groans and complaints from the room. Biggest groans of the night: when Marshall said diesel prices were high not because of the Iran war but the war in Ukraine, and when Marshall claimed he had objected to President Trump’s agenda “many times.”

Finally, I learned that Roger Marshall wasn’t the only one onstage with Great Bend ties. Greg Bauer, a local attorney, pointed out that the debate’s moderator, Fox 4’s John Holt, had roots here, too. “His father was a doctor here many years ago, and he grew up here,” Bauer said.

What the crowd thought

Mark Rondeau, a retired local attorney who helped organize the event, said he thought Hamilton held his own.

“But I just couldn’t wait for him to say, ‘Senator, let me introduce myself. My name is Adam Hamilton. You’re running against me. You’re not running against Chuck Schumer. You’re not running against Joe Biden. You’re not running against Kamala. You’re not running against Obama. I’m running against you.’ ”

“It’s just this effort to paint Hamilton as the most radical, left-wing, communist, Democrat, socialist,” Rondeau said. “That’s not who he is.”

Rondeau and his wife, Michelle, met the Marshalls years ago when Marshall’s family first moved to town.

“To be fair to him, I think he was trying to be a successful doctor and make a place for himself and his family here,” Michelle said. “But I think he always had his eye on something like this,” she said, nodding toward the TV.

“I’ll tell you this: I gave money to Roger Marshall when he ran for Congress, and I voted for him,” Mark said. “And then I watched what he did there, and he lost my vote, and he lost my support.”

Mandy Charles taught at Great Bend High School for 18 years and said she didn’t have any positive comments to share about her interactions with the Marshalls during that time. But she said she thought Marshall did better in the debate than she had expected going in.

“I think Hamilton’s closing argument was better than Marshall’s,” Charles said. (Hamilton closed by attacking Marshall over soaring diesel prices, cuts to SNAP and health care benefits, and ICE raids hurting southwest Kansas livestock operations.)

“I’m cautiously optimistic,” Charles added. “I want to believe in the blue wave, but I’m originally from Missouri, and I’ve been in Kansas since the mid-80s, and it’s just so red here. It’d be great if it happened. But I wouldn’t be surprised at all if it doesn’t.”

Andrea Bauer, a mom to young kids, also supported Marshall in his first Congressional run.

“We lent our names and helped with some fundraisers and things when he ran against (Tim) Huelskamp,” she said. “I thought he was one of us. I was hopeful that he would go to Washington advocating for our rural community.”

Marshall hasn’t, in her view. “So that’s why we’re adjusting course,” Bauer said, and supporting Hamilton in this race.

Bauer’s father-in-law, Greg, said he’d already voted early for Hamilton. “I wanted to make sure I got that done in case I died before November 3,” he said.

“I think what a lot of people in this room feel is that partisan solutions are not a long-term answer,” Greg said. “You have to have bipartisan solutions. Bob Dole knew that. Jerry Moran knows that. Kansans know that deep in their heart. But I don’t think Roger Marshall knows that.”

This story was originally published October 22, 2026 at 5:04 AM.
news.author: David Hudnall

news.title: Texas Latinos are turning on Trump. That doesn’t mean they’re sold on Democrats.
news.text:
EDINBURG — In years past, the march toward Election Day brought discord to Carlos Cancino’s home in Edinburg.

“My wife and I used to get into big old arguments during the elections, because she doesn’t like Trump,” Cancino said. “And I was a Trump supporter. We used to literally fight and not talk for, like, several days.”

But this year, Cancino, a Latino small-business owner in the Rio Grande Valley, has done a political 180. Angry over the state of the economy and high prices, he has soured on Trump — and plans to vote for Democrats.

“Now I can’t stand the guy,” Cancino said. “I can’t stand the Republican Party.”

Democrats’ success in Texas this cycle will hinge in large part on how many Latino voters have come to the same conclusion as Cancino, who’s part of a critical swing population in a state that suddenly finds itself, after decades of Republican control, home to a tossup U.S. Senate race. 

Just two years after major shifts in Latino voting patterns delivered President Donald Trump his largest ever margin of victory in Texas, affordability concerns and anger over the administration’s mass deportation campaign are fueling an expected swing back toward Democrats. 

The size of that swing, and where it shows up on the map, could decide whether Texas sends Ken Paxton or James Talarico to the U.S. Senate. And it will determine whether Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting pays off, after the Legislature redrew several congressional districts in majority-Hispanic South Texas with the intent of flipping them to GOP control.

But in interviews with over two dozen Latino strategists, organizers, candidates and voters in Texas, a common thread emerged: Any shift this year is less an embrace of the Democratic Party than a rebuke of the party in power — a reality that may persist for future elections with Latino voters established as a perpetual swing population.

“They’re not swinging back because they’re loving Democrats,” said Chuck Rocha, a Democratic strategist and Texas native working on numerous Democratic campaigns in the state. “They’re swinging back because Democrats are reminding them who broke it.”

In 2024, exit polls and precinct analyses estimate that Texas’ Latino vote split close to evenly between Democrat Kamala Harris and Trump. The shift was most evident in South Texas, where the president won all but two border counties and flipped major population centers like Cameron and Hidalgo counties for the first time in decades. Riding economic anxiety over inflation and persistent high prices, as well as frustration over migrant crossings at the southern border, Republicans at the top of the ticket hit new highs with Latino voters.

This fall’s election will test how solid the floor is. Latino Texans who loosened their ties to Democrats are not automatically coming home, strategists said, despite the discontent with Republicans captured in polling. Democratic candidates, saddled with a damaged party brand, will have to win over Latinos who feel let down by both parties, running on the strength of their own message.

“The conversations we’ve had at the doors with voters have very much implied that disillusionment with Republicans doesn’t translate into automatic Democratic support,” said Ricardo Rauseo, the national press secretary for Somos Votantes PAC, which is on the ground in several majority-Latino U.S. House districts in Texas. “Instead, they’re looking for candidates that are authentic and that are actively presenting and communicating a vision for the economy.”

Still, the GOP faces significant headwinds with Latino Texans that were not part of the picture two years ago. 

High costs remain a frustration — particularly gas prices in the aftermath of Trump’s decision to attack Iran, disrupting Middle Eastern oil flows. The border has quieted, a welcome change for many in South Texas. But the discussion around immigration politics has moved to the interior, where a spate of violent incidents involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including the shooting of a Latino man in Houston, have sparked allegations of anti-Hispanic racial profiling. In South Texas, ICE enforcement has also disrupted the local economy, especially the construction sector, a source of frustration in a growing region.

That combination has left Latino Texans angry at politicians writ large, said Mario Guerrero, a three-time Trump voter who will be voting for Democrats this cycle. Guerrero, the executive director of the South Texas Homebuilders Association, said that anger starts with Trump, who he said has made Latinos in South Texas feel deceived.

“I just feel like we need people to call out our politicians and just tell them to cut the crap,” Guerrero said. “We’re tired of this shit. We’re not your puppets, and that’s what they have us as right now.”

Amid this climate, polling has found Trump’s popularity taking a nosedive with Texas Latinos, 34% of whom said they approved of his job performance in an October CBS News poll. That was 11 percentage points below his overall standing in the state. 

That’s where Democrats’ economy-focused message is resonating with Latinos, Rocha said, adding that it’s landing because of the simple fact that they’re not in Trump’s party.

“The price of gas and groceries message is just where people are, and it’s the reason they’re swinging back,” he said.

A “Molotov cocktail” of enthusiasm

At a get-out-the-vote rally in Donna in early October, local Democratic candidates took to the microphone to hype up a mostly Latino crowd of hundreds. They were met with cheers when discussing their campaigns and loud boos when Trump or Gov. Greg Abbott came up. Multiple generations of families lined up for food and crowded around Democratic congressional candidate Bobby Pulido, a Tejano music star, when he arrived. The rallygoers were, to use the parlance of the internet, libbing out — South Texas style.

Speakers talked about how their candidates would represent la raza and argued that Republicans in Texas and Washington had corrupted the promise, instilled in them by their parents, of hard work paying off. And they implored attendees to vote.

“If we look at history, if we look at how people have voted in the past, it’s been very low percentage,” said Ricardo Rodriguez, the former Hidalgo County district attorney. “There’s a high amount of voter registration here in Hidalgo County. If us and El Paso would come out and vote during the early voting, man, it’s over. Texas will turn blue, ladies and gentlemen!”

For years, Democrats had banked on improving Latino turnout and the growth of the Hispanic population — now the largest demographic group in Texas — to deliver them majorities. But Republicans’ inroads with Latinos upended that prophecy.

This time, strategists and organizers see three trends that could finally break the GOP dam: dampened turnout among Latino Republicans, a sizable shift toward Democratic candidates among Latino Trump voters and heightened enthusiasm among Latino Democrats. That last trend will matter especially in the state’s major urban centers, where Democrats believe they can gain significant ground on turnout alone in places like Houston, San Antonio, Dallas and El Paso.

For a population that is younger and more working class than Texas as a whole, economic frustration and a sense of indignity over ICE is creating an unprecedented “Molotov cocktail” of enthusiasm, said Jaime Mercado, a Democratic strategist in Houston.

Just as important, if harder to see, is who is not talking about the election.

“There’s going to be a lot of folks who are just going to go to the polls, and frankly, just quietly make a mea culpa vote,” Mercado. “I personally know there’s people in my family who are not talking about it, they’re just giving me the quiet signal — I’m going to go make up for this.”

Whether or not that anger translates into votes for Democrats will be a decisive question for 2026. Strategists said they see Latino voters being driven more by individual candidates than party affiliation this cycle. 

Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of Equis, a Democratic-aligned firm which conducts research and polling on Latino voters, said people want to break with the party’s “brand” and “the past,” and successful Democratic candidates in South Texas “represent both of those things.”

“I actually think these guys represent a new brand of moderate anti-establishment candidates, that are bucking the brand and bucking the past, but are doing so in a kind of moderate and centrist way,” Valencia said.

The instinct to judge candidates beyond their party label is familiar to South Texas voters. Even amid the GOP’s historic performance in 2024, down-ballot Democrats in the region, including congressional candidates, won their races. Those outcomes showed Latino voters’ willingness to split their tickets and the Democratic Party’s enduring strength at the local level.

Equis’ September polling of likely Latino voters in Texas found an electorate poised to revert to the levels of support Beto O’Rourke won in 2018, when he captured 64% support from Latino Texans, according to exit polls. Talarico; state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor; and the generic congressional Democrat each received between 62% and 64% of the Latino vote. Other polls have been less rosy, suggesting a wide range of outcomes. Rocha projects the Texas Latino leftward swing will land between 10 and 25 percentage points.

In focus groups put on by Equis, numerous Texas Latino voters said they connected with Talarico’s faith and economic message, which centers on fixing high costs and a broken system in which the top earners have made it impossible for others to get ahead. Hinojosa, a Latina from the Valley, has been similarly razor-focused on the economy and corruption. And Pulido, with his celebrity and an economic message that celebrates building generational wealth rather than demonizing the rich, is among Democrats’ most prized recruits this cycle, and a candidate they believe can uniquely speak to Latino men, who shifted sharply to the right in 2024.

“For Democrats, the concern about Latino men and support there continues,” said Julián Castro, the former San Antonio mayor and U.S. housing secretary who now serves as the CEO of the Latino Community Foundation. “I think that they’re going to have to find ways to be able to connect with that community. They’ll do better in 2026, very likely, than they did in ‘24. But they have to build on that. Bobby Pulido can be helpful in that regard.”

Robert San Miguel, a political independent in Temple, is one such voter motivated by individual candidates. San Miguel voted for Trump in 2020 and in 2024, motivated in part by his support for tighter immigration policies. But he no longer backs the president, saying Trump lied about his commitment to keeping the United States out of foreign wars.

But San Miguel’s frustration does not make him a reliable Democratic vote. In the Senate race, he said he is disturbed by allegations of corruption against Paxton and will vote for Talarico, while planning to split his ticket. 

“I disagree with some of his views, but I actually think he’s a pretty decent person,” San Miguel said. Abbott, by contrast, has “not done anything horrible for Texas,” so San Miguel plans to stick with him.

The Republican pitch

Jorge Martinez, a Texas-based adviser and spokesperson for LIBRE Action, a conservative Latino voter outreach group, has spent 14 years organizing in the Rio Grande Valley, working to convince Latinos that the Republican Party — of low taxes, faith and protecting oil and gas jobs — should be their home.

“They’re natural conservatives,” Martinez said. “The thing here is that historically, it’s just because, oh, grandma voted this way, or mom voted this way. So people are just sticking to tradition or their custom. But we’ve seen some breakthroughs on that, where people broke through the party lines last cycle. But down ballot, they still voted Democrat.”

Martinez’s optimism this cycle comes from hearing the same candidate-over-party ethos Democrats are counting on. He sees it as an opportunity to break Democrats’ down-ballot hold on South Texas. While doorknocking for Republican congressional candidate Eric Flores, who is running in a majority-Hispanic seat from Brownsville to Corpus Christi, Martinez said he had conversations with six voters his group had identified as persuadable. Of those, he said four backed Flores. A fifth voter said little, and the sixth planned to vote for Democrat Vicente Gonzalez — but would have been open to Flores had he not received Trump’s endorsement.

The national environment, Martinez acknowledged, is an obstacle for the GOP.

“The challenge right now for Republicans is that they control the Congress, the Senate and the White House,” Martinez said. “[And] things are still expensive. They haven’t gone down like people had hoped for down here.”

Wayne Hamilton, a Republican operative who runs Project Red TX, a group focused on building GOP political power in South Texas, sees a similar anti-incumbent mood. He said it could simultaneously hurt Republicans in federal races and Democrats at the local level.

“In this particular election, there’s going to be voter retribution at all levels,” Hamilton said. “There’s no question about that, and it’s going to cut both ways.”

Hamilton compared Republican efforts in the region to the stock market: Some years are up, some years are down, but the overall trend, he believes, is positive. 

Hispanic Republican candidates in competitive majority-Hispanic South Texas districts, including Carlos and Monica De La Cruz, have at times leaned on their own working-class backgrounds on the trail, acknowledging they feel the pain of gas and grocery costs. They’ve also tried to tie their Democratic opponents to the most unpopular parts of former President Joe Biden’s agenda.

Other Republicans have doubled down on culture-war issues in their quest to keep Latino voters in the tent. Spanish language ads from pro-Paxton super PACs have made hay of Talarico’s viral comment that “God is nonbinary” and claimed he supports minors receiving gender transition procedures. Talarico has said his past comments on some culture war issues “missed the mark” and that he opposes gender reassignment surgery for minors. 

To be sure, Democrats and Republicans alike agree that the GOP’s gains with Latino voters, especially in South Texas, were not a mirage. Democrats say it’s unlikely they’ll return to their 2016-era margins, when Hillary Clinton won over 70% of the vote in places like Webb County, home to Laredo, and Starr County, home to Rio Grande City. 

“I think we’ve lost some forever, that will probably not come back,” said Jose Borjon, a Brownsville native who worked for six South Texas Democrats in Congress. “But I think the majority of them are persuadable — are people that can come to us. And I think what they’re seeing now — and these are people in their 30s, 40s and 50s — well, the economy’s not better. Gas prices have gone up. We’ve gone to war for reasons that we don’t really understand.”

Even if a blue wave materializes, several Latino Democrats cautioned the party against assuming its gains still stick. Of the Latinos who return to the Democratic fold, many will do so out of anger at Trump, Borjon said — and Democrats are benefiting from being the only viable alternative. 

Guerrero, the homebuilders’ association director who is voting for Democrats this cycle, said he expects Latinos to remain a swing vote as long as immigration and border policy continue to be used as political tools. 

“I think people are tired of both the right and the left,” Guerrero said. “I think we need peace. But what’s going to happen is, you’re going to see the pendulum swing from the right to the left. And when it swings that hard, we’re not going to be in the middle.”
news.summary: Latino strategists and voters say this year’s swing is driven by anger at those in power and hinges on individual candidates. Democrats and Republicans alike agree it may not last.
news.author: Gabby Birenbaum

news.title: What’s the Matter With Minnesota?
news.text:
With less than two weeks to go before the midterms, the tale is the same as it has been all fall: It’s hard to find anything going Republicans’ way. Look around. While the GOP’s super PACs continue flooding Senate races in red states like Texas, Ohio, Kansas, and Iowa with ads, Senate Democrats’ super PAC is investing in Mississippi. In the House, Republican election groups are retreating from lost causes to defend core seats.

But as Democrats put away House districts and Senate races in states like Georgia and North Carolina, one race is swimming curiously against the tide.

On the same day that the election handicappers at the Cook Political Report shifted their rating of the Mississippi and South Carolina Senate races in Democrats’ favor, and fellow forecasters at Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved dozens of House races Democrats’ way, Cook made another change. It moved the Minnesota Senate race, a contest between Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Republican former sports reporter Michele Tafoya, from “Likely Democrat” to “Lean Democrat.” Crystal Ball had made a similar decision the previous week. In other words, forecasters believe Flanagan is still the favorite, but not by much.

What’s going on here? Why, in a great environment for Democrats, and in a consistently blue state like Minnesota, is this race looking like a squeaker?

It’s not the same as New Hampshire, Democrats’ other misbehaving light-blue state that should be a shoo-in this year but somehow isn’t. In the Granite State, Republicans are running a former senator from the state’s Republican royal family, and Republican outside groups invested substantially, and early, in that race. Senate Republicans’ main super PAC, meanwhile, hasn’t put any money behind Tafoya’s bid; each candidate’s campaign has spent a civilized couple-million dollars each. And it’s not that Minnesota is a runaway train trending redder demographically. It’s dominated by the Twin Cities, and has a high percentage of adults with college degrees, the dividing line on which so much of Trump-era political realignment hinges.

Instead, Democrats’ inability to pull away in this race is a matter of candidate quality, and seismic news stories from Minnesota that garnered immense national attention.

It’s not that Flanagan, an energetic progressive who harnessed anti-D.C. energy to win her primary over the more moderate Rep. Angie Craig, is a dunderhead. But Flanagan—like other progressive-wing nominees such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine—is clawing tooth and nail to get over the finish line even in this ideal Democratic environment while more moderate candidates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Jon Ossoff in Georgia have effectively put their races away. If the energy brought by progressive candidates is outweighing the softness they might have with the median voter, that’s not being picked up in polling.

Tafoya, meanwhile, was mocked by many upon her entry to the race, as former Sunday Night Football sideline reporters don’t have substantial governing backgrounds. What former Sunday Night Football sideline reporters do have, though, is vast name recognition and an ability to speak well on TV. A lack of a substantial governing background has its advantages, too, as it allows her to draw up positions from scratch. She’s described herself as a “pro-choice Republican” (a posture that abortion rights advocates argue is not entirely on the level), has not had to take any votes on the Iran war, and has pledged to “stand up” to Trump when he’s wrong.

What sets the race apart, aside from positions here or there, though, is that Tafoya, more than the average 2026 Republican in Trump’s America, has a lot of offensive material to work with. Flanagan is lieutenant to Gov. Tim Walz, who presided over a state welfare fraud scandal of such magnitude that it ended his bid for a third term. Tafoya has made this her central line of attack, arguing that Flanagan should be held accountable for the failures of the administration.

“My opponent has been second in command in this state for eight years, drawing a taxpayer-funded paycheck,” Tafoya, in one of her many hits on Flanagan over the issue, said in a recent debate. “And what do we have to show for that? We have massive fraud, historic fraud. We have test scores down. We have crime spiking. We have a massive surplus turned into a deficit.”

Flanagan’s defense, meanwhile, is that the social services agencies responsible for being defrauded were outside her portfolio, and that the blame rests with Walz. “The governor’s been very clear that the buck stops with him,” Flanagan said during the debate, positioning the governor under the bus. “He was the one who had oversight here.”

Were that scandal to have been the last substantial national news story to explode out of Minnesota over the last year, Flanagan could be in even worse trouble. But it was the uncovering of those fraud scandals, along with its concentration of perpetrators within Minnesota’s Somali community, that egged the Trump administration into launching Operation Metro Surge, an assault on the Twin Cities from immigration enforcement authorities. That operation led to the deaths of two protesters under Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents’ heavy-handed tactics and turned the tide in both Minnesota and the nation against the administration’s mass deportation agenda.

It’s the legacy of Operation Metro Surge that will make it so challenging for Tafoya to turn the race into a true toss-up before Election Day. Trump’s heavy-handedness is not just an abstraction for Minnesota Democrats. They’ve battled it in their streets. If Tafoya’s task of hammering the welfare scandal is simple, Flanagan’s task—bringing up Trump, and the need to stop him—is simpler.

Earlier in the year, after she announced her candidacy, Tafoya said that she would be “honored” to have Trump’s endorsement, that she would “happily take” it. Trump has since become historically unpopular, and for a long time, she kept her distance. Just last week, though, Trump finally endorsed her, telling a crowd in Youngstown, Ohio (?), that “you have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who is a very respected person.” Trump said this with the briefest of pauses between “Michele” and “Tafoya,” as if he remembered in the moment that it might not be helpful to endorse her.

“I should say it,” he concluded anyway.

Tafoya’s reaction to the endorsement was telling. “I heard about that,” she said when asked about it. “Look, this campaign is about bringing all Minnesotans together, whether they voted for President Trump or whether they voted for Kamala Harris.” She was similarly evasive when asked during the debate about whether she would appear with Trump should he campaign in Minnesota—something he has threatened to do—twice giving responses that weren’t even in the ballpark of answering the question.

The RealClearPolitics polling average has Flanagan up 2 points over Tafoya at the moment, while an internal poll released by Senate Democrats’ super PAC, the Senate Majority PAC, at the beginning of the month showed her up by 8 points. Whatever it is, the same forecasters who are moving the race in Republicans’ direction “still believe the national environment will lift Flanagan to victory,” as the Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor put it.

It’s possible that the polls are way off, that Minnesota will fall in line with a result closer to what you’d expect, and that Flanagan wins in a walk. It’s just strange that we don’t know, particularly when, in much swingier states, Democrats have already seemingly clinched victory.

If the race is that tight, though, it’s a reminder that no “wave” election is ever uniform. Candidates matter, and state-specific issues matter. Weird things happen. In 2014, in an environment where Republicans won their largest House majority since the 1920s while picking up governor’s races in Maryland, Illinois, and Massachusetts, Democrats knocked off the incumbent GOP governor of Pennsylvania by 10 points. In 2018, when Democrats picked up 40 seats in the House, they lost a Florida Senate seat (and governor’s race) before the state had fully calcified into its present redness. There’s a not-unrealistic scenario in which Democrats win the Texas and Minnesota Senate seats by the same margin—or, if the polls are underestimating Republicans, lose them by the same margin.
