news.title: Trump hammers culture wars on campaign trail as economic pitch fizzles
news.text:
WASHINGTON – In a midterm election defined by Americans' pocketbook concerns, President Donald Trump veered off to a different topic as he spoke to supporters at a rally last week in Wasilla, Alaska.

"We will not let them cut our children," Trump said as he made a sharp cutting motion with his right hand. "It's called mutilization."

Trump was referring to gender-affirming surgeries, one of his go-to subjects to fire up the MAGA base. He then moved to another favorite attack on Democrats: transgender athletes in women's sports, spending several minutes telling stories of an undermatched female weightlifter and a swimmer who stood no chance against trans opponents.

"Who the hell ever thought we'd be fighting to keep men out of women's sports?" Trump said.

More: GOP troubles brew as Trump economic pitch clashes with voter sentiment

The material isn't new for Trump, who ran anti-trans advertisements in the 2024 election and targets the trans community often during public remarks. But now, in the homestretch to the Nov. 3 midterms, the president is leaning harder on his daily campaign swings into a familiar mix of hot-button, culturally divisive issues ‒ from fears about migrants and Islamophobia to "transgender insanity" ‒ despite polls showing the economy and cost of living are at the center of voters' minds.

The focus is part of a broader strategy for Trump during a weeks-long campaign blitz that has taken him to mostly deep-red areas in Republican-leaning states. It's not about winning over new voters to support Republican midterm candidates. The goal is to energize low-propensity voters who backed Trump in three presidential elections and ensure that they will turn out in November when Trump is not on the ballot.

"They expected him to fix the economy, and he hasn't. So if you don't have the No. 1 issue, you have to pivot to a different issue," said Todd Belt, director of the political management program at George Washington University. He said Trump and Republicans want to shift the midterms from a referendum on the president, whose approval ratings have reached all-time lows, to a "choice election" against Democrats.

"This is trying to define the Democratic candidates, who they are and what they stand for," Belt said.

More: Trump approval rating falls to career low in new poll

Trump's embrace of the culture wars comes as the president has struggled to convince Americans of an improving economy amid stubborn inflation and high gas prices caused by the U.S. war with Iran.

A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll last week found 75% of Americans believe the economy is poor. A poll this month from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found 65% of respondents blame Trump's policies for high costs more than other factors outside of his control. Seventy-three percent of Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the economy, according to the poll.

In the same speech in Alaska, Trump railed against Somali immigrants, saying they've "destroyed" and "fleeced" Minnesota. Trump urged Minnesotans to "fight back" against the Somali community in a recent social media post, accusing them of being responsible for "Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State."

Trump pivoted to the Second Amendment at a rally in Dalton, Georgia. "He's going to take away your guns," Trump said, referring to Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is running against Republican Rep. Mike Collins.

And during a campaign rally in Youngstown, Ohio, Trump called Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, a "jihadist." He accused "radical left maniacs" of trying to take away Christopher Columbus Day. He also took aim at Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, saying, "they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone."

"He's trying to use sort of a 'bandwagon effect' for his voters, to get them out, to energize the base," Belt said. "There's a lot of talk about how unpopular he is, and he's trying to counter that narrative by doing these rallies and playing the 'greatest hits,' as we would say, with immigration and the social issues."

Anti-trans rhetoric remains go-to attack

As he moves from one state to the next in his midterm blitz, Trump has not ignored the economy as a talking point. But instead of appealing to cost-of-living anxieties, he's mocked the term "affordability" as a creation of Democrats, falsely claimed inflation is down and touted the economy as the greatest in American history.

More than any other wedge issue, Trump and Republicans are betting on anti-trans rhetoric to try to stave off a blue wave. Democrats are widely favored to win control of the House of Representatives in the midterms, and close Senate races in several traditionally Republican states point to a potential Democratic takeover of the Senate as well.

Since Aug. 1, Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups have spent more than $100 million ahead of the midterms airing 200 ads that reference transgender issues, according to AdImpact, a firm that tracks political advertising.

More: Is a midterm blue wave for Democrats becoming a blue tsunami?

Trump recently referred to South Carolina Democratic Senate nominee Annie Andrews by the anti-trans slur "Trannie" in a social media post.

During a stop in Kalispell, Montana, Trump accused Democratic congressional candidate Sam Forstag, who is running in a fiercely contested House race in the state, of personally fighting for the "transgender mutilization of Montana children (and) drag shows in Montana." The attack appeared to be a reference to Forstag's past work as a lobbyist for the ACLU.

"Does anybody like the idea of his paying for drag shows in Montana schools?" Trump said.

At multiple rallies, Trump has also singled out WNBA player Sophie Cunningham, who has been lauded on the right for her vocal opposition to trans athletes in women's sports. In Ohio, Trump called Cunningham a "beautiful young woman" and remarked to former NFL coach Jon Gruden, who was stumping for Trump at the event, "You probably wouldn't mind her on the team, not to help with points, but with attendance."

He followed it up by sharing on his Truth Social account a well-known photo of Cunningham pointing her finger at a basketball opponent.

More: 'Clowns are out.' Hegseth lashes out at trans troops, 'beardos' in speech

At the same time, anti-trans ads have flooded the airwaves of midterm battleground states, where large donors and PAC money have given Republican Senate candidates a significant edge in television advertising.

A Senate Leadership Fund ad accuses Ohio Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown of supporting sex changes for minors, citing an interview he gave in 2023 in which he said “a child’s health care decisions are between them, their parents, their families, their doctors – not politicians."

In Texas, ads funded by a PAC aligned with Senate Republican nominee Ken Paxton accuse Democrat James Talarico of supporting the use of "taxpayer dollars for sex change surgeries on young children.” The misleading ad references Talarico's vote as a state representative against legislation to broadly prohibit gender-affirming care, yet it does not mention that he voted for an amendment that sought to narrow the bill to ban surgeries.

Not all Republicans are on board with culture-war strategy

Trump relied heavily on anti-trans ads ahead of his 2024 election victory over Democrat Kamala Harris. But transgender rights groups predict they won't resonate with voters in next month's midterms.

“Voters are growing tired of the same recycled anti-trans attacks they’ve now seen for three consecutive election cycles," said Ramiro Sarmiento, national press secretary for the Human Rights Campaign. He said that while Republicans have pumped millions into ads focused on the transgender community, they've failed to address "what voters actually care about" ‒ the rising cost of living, gas prices, groceries and political corruption.

"With no solutions to offer, all Republicans have left is to manufacture a culture war that scapegoats the trans community to distract from their own failures," Sarmiento said.

More: Republicans jump ship as Trump's anchor weighs heavy on party

A CNN/SSRS poll in September found transgender policies rank below 10 other issues in terms of importance for voters, with only 25% calling it "extremely important." Leading the way was the economy, with 68% of voters saying the issue is "extremely important."

Some Republicans are also skeptical about campaigning too aggressively on culture wars.

Texas state Rep. Dade Phelan, a former Republican speaker of the Texas House, questioned the effectiveness of an onslaught of anti-trans ads attacking Talarico and other Democrats in Texas, in addition to other Republican ads focused on "defund the police," "boys in girls sports" and Chinese investments in Texas land.

"This is messaging you do in a primary ‒ a real red meat, Republican knock-down, drag-out fight," Phelan told USA TODAY, though he theorized that the ads could help erase the enthusiasm gap Republicans face against Democrats in the midterms.

"But otherwise, I think the downside is it could be turning off the 10% of Texans who are going to decide this election. Those are your moderate voters, your swing voters, your lower-propensity voters, that are probably more motivated by the economy and cost-of-living," he said.

More: Texas ad messages shift as Paxton, Talarico take pitches on tour

Phelan, a Paxton critic who plans not to vote in the Texas Senate race, said the ads are focused on "stuff that is just not occurring" in most Texas communities.

"In southeast Texas, I've never seen a boy play in girls sports. And quite frankly, no one knows anyone who can afford a transgender surgery," Phelan said. "You can run the risk of looking very out of touch."

Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster and strategist, said the avalanche of anti-trans and other cultural attacks are unlikely to prove as potent for Republicans in the 2026 midterms as they did in the 2024 election.

"Right now, the cultural issues that worked in 2024 are being overwhelmed by economic issues of inflation, economic growth and concern about tariffs, and the effect on the war on Iran," Ayres said. "So, the cultural issues are still present but they don't carry the same juice."

Meanwhile, with two weeks until an election that increasingly seems to favor Democrats, Trump this week found a new hot-button issue to pounce on: mass protests in France over education and the cost of living. Trump blamed unconstrained immigration in France for the riots, warning that the U.S. could be next if Democrats are put in control.

"If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what's happening in France," Trump said in an Oct. 19 rally in Park City, Kansas. "A once-great nation that is being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity. And they hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself.

"They're destroying that country, and we're not going to let that happen to this country," Trump said.

Reach Joey Garrison on X @joeygarrison.

news.title: Senate Republicans on Defensive in Unexpected States as Midterms Enter Final Weeks
news.text:
With the midterm elections around two weeks away, Senate Republicans are finding themselves playing defense in some unexpected places as Democrats continue to chip away at their hold in the polls.

Most observers for the past year have expected that Democrats would reclaim the House, boosted by historical trends such as the presidential “six-year itch,” which favor the out-of-power party, and by diminishing approval for congressional Republicans.

But few observers expected Democrats to reclaim the Senate following Republicans’ sweep of the upper chamber in 2024, when the GOP picked up four seats for a total of 53.

That’s changing as Democrats make polling gains in key Senate races.

Here’s what to know.

Perhaps the most watched race of the entire cycle is in Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has maintained a consistent and compelling lead over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton across the election cycle.

For decades, Democrats in the Lone Star State have dreamed of “turning Texas blue.”

They came close in the 2018 race against Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), when Democratic nominee Beto O’Rourke came within around 2.5 percentage points of unseating the incumbent.

Then, in 2024, President Donald Trump swept the state by 14 points. For many Democrats, that seemed to be the end of their hopes to flip the state.

But now, the race is devouring Senate Republicans’ funding as Talarico has consistently led in polls, with downstream effects on funding for Republicans across the country.

Talarico has built a campaign based on his values as a liberal Presbyterian seminarian and on his track record as a state legislator, leading in 18 out of the 19 polls conducted since July. Paxton has led in a single poll conducted by Emerson College.

In a sign of the party’s growing electoral woes, Republicans in early October pulled funding out of former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley’s Senate race against former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper entirely.

Polls have shown Cooper favored this cycle, leading in every poll since July 2025. Cooper leads by around 9.2 percentage points, based on an average of the six most recent polls.

North Carolina has long been seen in national politics as a purple state—but one inclined, in most cases, to favor Republicans. Still, some recent elections have been nail-biters for Republicans.

Trump himself has acknowledged concerns about his handpicked candidate’s struggles in North Carolina.

“I am worried about him,” Trump told reporters Friday as he left for an Alabama campaign rally. “I hope he wins.”

In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is favored by observers and polling to hold onto his seat in the blue-shifting state, leading Republican nominee Rep. Mike Collins by 7.6 percentage points in an average of five recent polls.

As the Atlanta metropolitan area has grown, the state as a whole has trended increasingly toward Democrats in recent years, beginning with President Joe Biden’s victory over Trump in 2020. In 2024, amid a favorable national environment, Trump reclaimed Georgia by about 2.2 percentage points—Republicans’ lowest margin of victory in the Peach State since 1996.

There are also warning signs for Republicans in Great Plains states such as Kansas and Nebraska.

Kansans have long been known in national politics for their deeply Republican voting tendencies.

But in recent years, some observers began to notice a rising purple streak in the state’s national voting habits that could boost Democrat Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist megachurch pastor and author who’s making a competitive showing in polls against incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

Marshall is an obstetrician-gynecologist who was first elected in 2020 after beating out a crowded primary field. He’s been the subject of controversy in the state after The New York Times reported that he had sued hundreds of his former patients over unpaid medical bills, leading to 81 arrests due to missed court dates.

Marshall has decried the report as a political hit job, saying he used standard billing practices and maintaining that he has delivered thousands of babies free of charge to lower-income families.

The race was originally rated lean Republican by Cook Political Report, which now rates it a toss-up. Although Marshall led in the first poll taken of the race released on Sept. 11, every poll since has shown him either tied with or running behind Hamilton, and Republicans appear to be worried.

The funding pulled from North Carolina has been pushed into the Kansas race by national Republicans. Trump spoke in support of Marshall at a rally near Wichita on Oct. 19.

In 2020, key population centers such as Shawnee County—which houses Topeka, the capital—and Riley County backed the Democrat in the Senate and presidential races for the first time since the 1970s.

Much will come down to Johnson County, a Kansas City suburb lying just west of the border with Missouri, and by far the single most important county in state politics, making up around one-fifth of the state’s entire population.

For years, it’s been shifting left, backing both Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris in the previous two elections.

In Nebraska, independent candidate Dan Osborn—who made national news following his close fight against Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) in 2024—is making another bid for the office.

This year, he’s running against Republican incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts, and polls have shown a tight race. In surveys taken in September and October, Ricketts led by 4 and 5 points, respectively. Osborn led by about the same margin in polls taken in May and September.

Republicans maintain a structural advantage in the state. Although 53 percent of registered Nebraska voters live in rural areas, the urban and suburban population in Nebraska is reliably Republican—but could swing in line with an anti-Republican national environment.

Omaha is a crucial decision-maker in the race, as its population has trended away from Republicans in recent cycles, voting for Harris in 2024.

In another shift, Republicans are moving $5 million into Sen. Darline Graham’s (R-S.C.) race against physician Annie Andrews.

Graham was appointed to the seat by outgoing Gov. Henry McMaster earlier this year, following her brother Lindsey Graham’s death in July.

The $5 million investment into the race is significant as the state has rarely needed such funding from the national party in the past, though it’s not an amount that necessarily signals alarm.

Currently, Graham leads in all three polls taken of the race, but the margins are rather narrow in a state that backed Trump by around 18 percentage points just two years ago.

On average, Graham sits at 44.7 percent in polls. Andrews, running as a moderate Democrat in the Republican stronghold, has 43.3 percent support, trailing Graham but well within the margin of error.

Trump is scheduled to visit the state as part of his blitz of midterm campaign rallies.

Though it’s almost forgotten now, Iowa and Ohio were—as recently as 2012—seen as quintessential political battlegrounds.

Both states have been seen as reliably Republican over the past several cycles, ever since Trump won them back from Democrats in 2016 with a nearly 10-point victory in Iowa and an 8-point victory in Ohio.

But this year, Senate races in the Midwest states are proving competitive, raising the prospect that the states could be on the cusp of returning to their swing-state status.

In Iowa, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is facing off with state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democrat, after Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) declined to run for a third term. Hinson has led in five polls conducted of the race since April, while Turek has led in four, and Cook Political Report recently moved the race from “lean Republican” to a toss-up.

In Ohio, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is set for a November fight against incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Brown has led in all 10 polls conducted in the state since July, excluding one poll that showed the race tied.

A key concern for both states has been farming prices, as farmers have widely reported financial difficulties amid the international tariffs imposed by Trump.

news.title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'
news.text:
BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from "Trump Won" caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99.

Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn't as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.

At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall, a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot.

"He's no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked," said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, "Dumb and Dumber."

Trump's lame duck status isn't the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump's average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %.

Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president's approval rating had fallen five more points.

Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE's massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags.

"People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election," said Hays, 80.

When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.

"After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done," said Hays. "They didn't have to promote MAGA or Trump."

Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He's waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future.

Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn't inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he's a salesman - and he tells people what they want to hear.

Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation.

In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he's trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He's concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer.

news.title: Elon Musk threatens Hillary Clinton's podcast partner Kara Swisher with prison after she claimed to know 'what's coming for him' if Democrats take power
news.text:
The world's richest man, Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, threatened the podcast partner of former First Lady Hillary Clinton with prison in a recent X post.

With the midterm elections approaching in what is projected to be a 'blue wave' victory for Democrats, the Trump ally appears to have little tolerance for criticism and fired online against tech journalist Kara Swisher.

Swisher, who launched the High Stakes podcast with Hillary Clinton just last week, appeared on another podcast, The Bulwark.

In a recent episode, Swisher suggested that Democrats should look into investigating Musk should they manage to gain control of both chambers of Congress in November.

She even went so far as to say that Musk would already have been sent to jail if Trump's Democratic challenger Kamala Harris had won the presidential election in 2024.

'Under Kamala Harris, he might be in jail right now, right?' Swisher suggested. 'And that's not because she's some avenging fury. It's because there is a lot of questions around different companies of his.'

She further claimed that the agencies affected by the cuts Musk made when he was running the Department of Government Efficiency would start investigating his many companies. 

Swisher continued: 'If Donald Trump loses the Senate, I would be worried if I were him even though how rich he is.

'He has a very big sense of fate. And I think it's coming for him. And real hard.' 

The furious world's first trillionaire took his upset with Swisher's comments to social media and posted on X: 'Live by the sword, die by the sword.

'Sounds like Swisher really wants to go to prison.' 

While the excerpt of Swisher's comments reached more than 2.4 million views on X, Musk's comment underneath got about 574,000 views as of Wednesday night and sparked strong reactions.

One asked: 'Why would he be in jail for? He hasn't broken the law.'

Another calmed down the entrepreneur, saying: 'No worries, Kamala is NEVER going to be President.'

Polls are projecting that next month's Midterm elections could hand the Democrats both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Meanwhile, top Republicans insist those surveys are skewed and that the GOP will do far better than predicted.

The Daily Mail contacted Swisher for comment. 

Musk has poured more than $276 million into Republican groups as the party faces a challenging environment in advance of the midterm elections. 

The development comes as it was reported Musk ordered a reduction in Starlink satellite services for Ukraine even as the tech billionaire claimed any limits on the communications system would ultimately have come from the president. 

Musk capped the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the system, making some of Kyiv's drones useless, the Wall Street Journal reported. 

Kyiv has accused Washington of deliberately slowing speeds at which Starshield – a Starlink satellite network for national security services – can be used effectively, a charge denied last week by US President Donald Trump.

Musk had previously said that 'any limits on speed or usage' of Starshield systems were 'decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS', referring to Mr Trump.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Washington had no prior knowledge of the slowdown.

'The President has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,' Mr Rubio said during his trip to India.

'That's a private company; the President doesn't run that company and can't direct that company to do anything... I'm telling you, there was no foreknowledge.'

On Tuesday, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the Pentagon had not directed any changes to Starshield, saying: 'We haven't pulled anything back.
news.summary: With the midterm elections approaching in what is projected to be a 'blue wave,' the Trump ally appears to have little tolerance for criticism and fired online against tech journalist Kara Swisher.

news.title: What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
news.text:
Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.

Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics: More than 100 million people likely will cast ballots in this year’s midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022; and as of October 12, a record $3.8 billion had been spent on political advertisements that have been aired so far.

Top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan, according to AdImpact, which tracks the activities.

Elon Musk alone has spent about $366m to support Republicans, according to campaign finance records.

Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155m votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example.

Control of Congress at stake

Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress.

Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.

Democrats are also fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.

Can midterms affect the presidency?

Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026, that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.

The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president’s performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.

Midterm election results can also give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.

What are polls showing?

Approval of Trump’s performance is at an all-time low of 32 per cent, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.

At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans. If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.

There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump’s immigration enforcement tactics.

However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued scepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.

Recent midterm history

Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.

In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama’s landmark healthcare reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.

The Republican wave was a “shellacking,” Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defence spending.

Democrats returned the favour in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.

This year’s elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in their state-level legislative bodies.Currently, Republicans control 55pc of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8pc, according to Ballotpedia.

Who will be speaker?

If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker second in line for the presidency after the vice president is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader.

Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called “unprecedented levels of corruption” during the Trump administration.

Jeffries also would steer Democrats’ legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.

A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker’s gavel remains in that party’s hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defence spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill.”

Marquee races

Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler’s bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran.

Also high on Democrats’ list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.

Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.

Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.

news.title: Texas turncoats: Another Bush scion turns on the Republicans in Lone Star State... days after Jenna Bush Hager's sister donated thousands to James Talarico
news.text:
Another member of America's most famous Republican dynasty has dramatically broken ranks with his own party, revealing he voted for a Democrat in Texas's fiercely contested Senate race while delivering a blistering attack on Donald Trump.

Neil Bush, the brother of former President George W. Bush and son of former President George H.W. Bush, announced on Tuesday that he had cast his ballot for Democrat James Talarico rather than Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton.

The political defection comes just days after reports that Barbara Pierce Bush, the twin sister of Today show host Jenna Bush Hager, donated thousands of dollars to Talarico's campaign.

It marks another striking departure from Republican loyalties within a family whose name has been synonymous with conservative politics in Texas for decades.

While announcing his vote, Neil Bush accused Trump and those who supported him of inflicting 'enormous damage to the Republican Party.'

In an unusually candid Facebook statement, Bush explained that his decision was driven by serious concerns about Paxton, Texas's controversial attorney general, and admiration for his Democratic opponent.

'My vote was motivated by two things: deep concern about Ken Paxton's record and genuine admiration for the character and principles I see in James Talarico,' he wrote.

The announcement lands at a particularly sensitive moment for Republicans as early voting began on Monday in a Senate contest that could see Democrats pull off a historic victory in a state they have struggled to win for nearly four decades.

Bush, whose family helped transform Texas into a Republican stronghold, acknowledged that he was abandoning his usual political allegiance.

He said he had been a 'Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles.'

But he insisted that loyalty to the party could no longer outweigh his concerns about the candidates.

'But character matters more than party affiliation,' Bush declared.

'Our democracy depends on leaders who respect our institutions, tell the truth, accept accountability, and seek to unite rather than divide.'

Neil insists his decision is about more than simply opposing the Republican candidate.

'I've never met James Talarico, but I have been enormously impressed by the way he approaches complicated and controversial issues,' he wrote.

'He speaks with respect, seeks common ground, and seems genuinely interested in bringing people together rather than driving them apart.'

Bush also praised Talarico's religious convictions, describing the Democratic candidate's faith as an important part of his character.

He said he recognized in Talarico 'the qualities I admire most in public servants: integrity, civility, humility, and a willingness to listen to those with whom he disagrees.'

His criticism of Paxton was particularly pointed.

Bush said he was 'deeply troubled by Paxton's conduct as Texas Attorney General, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power.'

Paxton played a prominent role in efforts to contest the 2020 election results, bringing a lawsuit challenging the outcome in four battleground states. The Supreme Court rejected the case.

The attorney general has also faced years of legal and political controversy.

He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015, although the criminal case was eventually resolved through a diversion agreement.

In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached him over separate allegations involving bribery and abuse of office.

Paxton denied wrongdoing and was subsequently acquitted by the state Senate, allowing him to remain in office.

Despite those controversies, he emerged victorious from a bitter Republican Senate primary earlier this year, defeating longtime incumbent John Cornyn after securing Trump's endorsement.

The president has since thrown his political weight behind Paxton, repeatedly visiting Texas to campaign for him.

But Neil Bush's intervention suggests that even the endorsement of a sitting Republican president has not been enough to keep every member of the party's most celebrated Texas family onside.

The political split within the Bush family comes after another member of the dynasty publicly backed Talarico with her checkbook.

Barbara Pierce Bush, George W. Bush's daughter and Neil Bush's niece, contributed $2,500 to Lone Star Rising PAC, a political action committee supporting the Democratic candidate.

Federal Election Commission records show the donation was made on September 23, although it only attracted widespread attention after being reported on October 16.

Barbara, 44, is the twin sister of NBC morning television personality Jenna Bush Hager and the granddaughter of the late President George H.W. Bush.

Her decision to financially support a Democrat was particularly striking given her family's role in building the modern Republican Party in Texas.

Barbara has previously supported Democrats, including campaigning for Kamala Harris in 2024, and has said she does not identify with either major political party.

The endorsement from the Bushes comes as Democrats sense a rare opportunity to break the Republican stranglehold on Texas's Senate seats.

The Lone Star State has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1988, but recent polling has suggested an unusually competitive contest between Talarico and Paxton.

A CBS News poll placed Talarico narrowly ahead, although the network's Battleground Tracker continues to classify the race as a toss-up.
news.summary: Neil Bush has broken ranks with his Republican dynasty, revealing he voted for Democrat James Talarico in Texas's fiercely contested Senate race.
news.author: Editor,James Gordon
